```{r gating-figures-defs}
)

gate_defs <- list(
    list(id = 1, dir = "gate1_lymphocytes", title = "Gate 1: Lymphocytes (FSC-A vs SSC-A)",
         pool = GATE_ALL8, xcol = "FSC-A", ycol = "SSC-A", xcof = NA, ycof = NA, split = NULL, partial = TRUE),
    list(id = 2, dir = "gate2_singlets", title = "Gate 2: Single cells (FSC-A vs FSC-H)",
         pool = GATE_ALL8, xcol = "FSC-A", ycol = "FSC-H", xcof = NA, ycof = NA, split = NULL, partial = TRUE),
    list(id = 3, dir = "gate3_CD45_CD14", title = "Gate 3: CD45+CD14- leukocytes (CD14 vs CD45)",
         pool = GATE_ALL8, xcol = "CD14", ycol = "CD45", xcof = 150, ycof = 150, split = NULL, partial = TRUE),
    list(id = 4, dir = "gate4_CD45_CD19", title = "Gate 4: B cells (CD19 vs CD45)",
         pool = GATE_ALL8, xcol = "CD19", ycol = "CD45", xcof = 150, ycof = 150,
         split = list(pos = POP_B, label = c("CD19+ (B cells)", "CD19-")), partial = FALSE),
    list(id = 5, dir = "gate5_CD3_CD56", title = "Gate 5: NK vs T cells (CD56 vs CD3)",
         pool = setdiff(GATE_ALL8, POP_B), xcol = "CD56", ycol = "CD3", xcof = 150, ycof = 150,
         split = list(pos = POP_NK, label = c("CD3-CD56+ (NK cells)", "CD3+ (T cells)")), partial = FALSE),
    list(id = 6, dir = "gate6_CD4_CD8", title = "Gate 6: CD4+ vs CD8+ T cells (CD4 vs CD8)",
         pool = setdiff(GATE_ALL8, c(POP_B, POP_NK)), xcol = "CD4", ycol = "CD8", xcof = 150, ycof = 150,
         split = list(pos = c(POP_NA_CD8, POP_EM_CD8, POP_TE_CD8), label = c("CD8+", "CD4+")), partial = FALSE),
    list(id = 7, dir = "gate7_CCR7_CD45RA_CD4", title = "Gate 7: CD4+ T-cell subsets (CD45RA vs CCR7)",
         pool = c(POP_EM_CD4, POP_NA_CD4, POP_TE_CD4), xcol = "CD45RA", ycol = "CCR7", xcof = 150, ycof = 150,
         split = list(multi = TRUE), partial = FALSE),
    list(id = 8, dir = "gate8_CCR7_CD45RA_CD8", title = "Gate 8: CD8+ T-cell subsets (CD45RA vs CCR7)",
         pool = c(POP_NA_CD8, POP_EM_CD8, POP_TE_CD8), xcol = "CD45RA", ycol = "CCR7", xcof = 150, ycof = 150,
         split = list(multi = TRUE), partial = FALSE)
)

gating_disp <- function(x, b) asinh(x / b)

gating_make_plot <- function(d, gate, donor_id) {
    sub <- d[d$donor == donor_id & d$population %in% gate$pool, ]
    x <- sub[[gate$xcol]]; y <- sub[[gate$ycol]]
    if (!is.na(gate$xcof)) x <- gating_disp(x, gate$xcof)
    if (!is.na(gate$ycof)) y <- gating_disp(y, gate$ycof)
    df <- data.frame(x = x, y = y, population = sub$population)

    if (is.null(gate$split)) {
        p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
            geom_hex(bins = 100) +
            scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "turbo", trans = "log10", name = "cells")
    } else if (isTRUE(gate$split$multi)) {
        multi_levels <- c("Naive CD4", "EM CD4", "TEMRA CD4", "Naive CD8", "EM CD8", "TEMRA CD8")
        df$label <- factor(gate_pop_short[df$population], levels = intersect(multi_levels, gate_pop_short))
        p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = label)) +
            geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.25) +
            scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = NULL) +
            guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1)))
    } else {
        df$label <- factor(
            ifelse(df$population %in% gate$split$pos, gate$split$label[1], gate$split$label[2]),
            levels = gate$split$label
        )
        p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = label)) +
            geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.2) +
            scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("red3", "grey50"), gate$split$label), name = NULL) +
            guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1)))
    }

    subtitle <- sprintf(
        "donor%d, n = %s cells%s", donor_id, format(nrow(sub), big.mark = ","),
        if (isTRUE(gate$partial)) " (surviving branch only -- excluded cells were not exported)" else ""
    )
    p + labs(title = gate$title, subtitle = subtitle,
             x = sprintf("%s%s", gate$xcol, if (!is.na(gate$xcof)) sprintf(" (asinh/%d)", gate$xcof) else ""),
             y = sprintf("%s%s", gate$ycol, if (!is.na(gate$ycof)) sprintf(" (asinh/%d)", gate$ycof) else "")) +
        theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
        theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7.5))
}

gating_fig_root <- file.path(out_dir, "figures", "gating")
for (gate in gate_defs) {
    gdir <- file.path(gating_fig_root, gate$dir)
    dir.create(gdir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    for (donor_id in 1:7) {
        outfile <- file.path(gdir, sprintf("donor%d.png", donor_id))
        if (!file.exists(outfile)) {
            p <- gating_make_plot(gating_data, gate, donor_id)
            ggsave(outfile, p, width = 5.5, height = 4.2, dpi = 150)
        }
    }
}
cat("Gating figures written under", gating_fig_root, "\n")
```

Each gate's 7 per-donor plots are composed into a single 3-per-row contact
sheet with `magick::image_montage()` rather than relying on knitr's
`fig.show = "hold"` layout, which tiles reliably in HTML but not in the
`xelatex` PDF output this document also renders to. The individual per-donor
PNGs above remain on disk under `r file.path(out_dir, "figures", "gating")`
for anyone who wants a single figure rather than the grid.

```{r gating-figures-display, results = "asis", eval =FALSE}
stopifnot(requireNamespace("magick", quietly = TRUE))
for (gate in gate_defs) {
    cat(sprintf("\n### %s\n\n", gate$title))
    gdir <- file.path(gating_fig_root, gate$dir)
    files <- file.path(gdir, sprintf("donor%d.png", 1:7))
    grid_file <- file.path(gdir, "grid_3col.png")
    if (!file.exists(grid_file)) {
        imgs <- magick::image_read(files)
        montage <- magick::image_montage(imgs, tile = "3x3", geometry = "x450+8+8", bg = "white")
        magick::image_write(montage, grid_file, format = "png")
    }
    cat(sprintf("![%s](%s)\n\n", gate$title, grid_file))
}
```

## Metrics

Each function is documented because every number in the results flows through
it.

A fixed random subset of cells is used for the ambiguity calculation in every
run (the full distance matrix would not fit in memory), so ambiguity values are
comparable across configurations.

```{r amb-idx}
set.seed(99)
amb_idx <- sort(sample(N, min(params$n_amb, N)))
```

```{r metric-functions}
#' Adjusted Rand index between two partitions.
#'
#' Thin wrapper around mclust::adjustedRandIndex(). With n_ij the number of
#' cells in cluster i of partition A and class j of partition B, the ARI is
#'   (sum_ij C(n_ij,2) - E) / (0.5 * (sum_i C(a_i,2) + sum_j C(b_j,2)) - E),
#' where E = sum_i C(a_i,2) * sum_j C(b_j,2) / C(n,2) is the number of agreeing
#' pairs expected under random assignment with the same cluster sizes.
#' Range: ~0 for chance, 1 for identical partitions, negative if worse than chance.
#' Invariant to relabelling, so metacluster numbers need not match populations.
ari_score <- function(a, b) mclust::adjustedRandIndex(a, b)

#' Node purity: fraction of cells that belong to the majority known population
#' of the SOM node they were mapped to. 1 = every node is pure. This is
#' deliberately NOT adjusted for the number of nodes: it rises trivially with
#' more nodes, so compare it only at a fixed grid size.
node_purity <- function(node, pop) {
    tab <- table(node, pop)
    sum(apply(tab, 1, max)) / length(node)
}

#' Distance of every cell to every SOM code vector, for FlowSOM's `distf`.
#'   1 = Manhattan  sum_p |x_p - c_p|
#'   2 = Euclidean  sqrt(sum_p (x_p - c_p)^2)
#'   3 = Chebyshev  max_p |x_p - c_p|
#'   4 = cosine     1 - <x, c> / (||x|| ||c||)
#' @param X cells x markers
#' @param codes nodes x markers
#' @return cells x nodes matrix
node_distances <- function(X, codes, distf) {
    n <- nrow(X); K <- nrow(codes)
    if (distf == 4) {
        eps <- .Machine$double.eps
        nx <- pmax(sqrt(rowSums(X^2)), eps)
        nc <- pmax(sqrt(rowSums(codes^2)), eps)
        return(1 - (X / nx) %*% t(codes / nc))
    }
    D <- matrix(0, n, K)
    for (j in seq_len(K)) {
        diff <- X - rep(codes[j, ], each = n)      # column-major recycling: one value per marker
        D[, j] <- switch(as.character(distf),
            "1" = rowSums(abs(diff)),
            "2" = sqrt(rowSums(diff^2)),
            "3" = rowMaxs(abs(diff)),
            stop("unsupported distf"))
    }
    D
}

#' Cluster ambiguity of cells, as in CySA's "Cluster ambiguity" tab, generalised
#' to any of the four distances.
#'
#' For each cell: own = distance to the code vector of the node it was assigned
#' to; rival = distance to the nearest *other* node. The ratio own/rival is
#' <= 1 for a correctly assigned cell. A ratio near 1 means the node boundary
#' does not really separate the cell from its neighbour. A cell is called
#' "ambiguous" when the ratio exceeds 0.9. The ratio is scale-free, so the
#' threshold means the same under rescaling of the data, but ratios of
#' different distance functions are not strictly comparable with one another.
#'
#' The node assignment `node` is computed by the run engine under the SOM's
#' training distance (see "The run engine"), so own/rival are consistent with it.
#' @param X training matrix (cells x markers), in the space the SOM was trained in
#' @param codes SOM code book (nodes x markers)
#' @param node integer node assignment per cell
#' @param idx cell subset to evaluate (memory)
ambiguity_metrics <- function(X, codes, node, distf, idx) {
    D <- node_distances(X[idx, , drop = FALSE], codes, distf)
    own_j <- node[idx]
    n <- length(idx)
    own <- D[cbind(seq_len(n), own_j)]
    D[cbind(seq_len(n), own_j)] <- Inf
    rival <- rowMins(D)
    ratio <- own / pmax(rival, .Machine$double.eps)
    list(pct_ambiguous = 100 * mean(ratio > 0.9),
         median_ratio = median(ratio))
}

#' FlowSOM's own consensus metaclustering of the SOM code vectors.
#' Run inside tempdir() so any file output of ConsensusClusterPlus cannot
#' collide between parallel workers.
meta_cluster <- function(codes, k, seed) {
    old <- setwd(tempdir()); on.exit(setwd(old), add = TRUE)
    FlowSOM::metaClustering_consensus(codes, k = k, seed = seed)
}

#' Between-population variance fraction (eta^2) of every column of X:
#' eta^2 = SS_between / SS_total. 1 = the marker is perfectly explained by
#' population, 0 = no information about population.
#' ORACLE: uses the known labels, so only meaningful as a diagnostic or an
#' upper bound, never for unlabeled data.
eta2 <- function(X, grp) {
    gs <- rowsum(X, grp)
    ng <- as.numeric(table(grp)[rownames(gs)])
    gm <- gs / ng
    mu <- colMeans(X)
    ss_between <- colSums(ng * sweep(gm, 2, mu, "-")^2)
    ss_total   <- colSums(X^2) - nrow(X) * mu^2
    ss_between / ss_total
}
```

How to read the scores, and their traps:

* **ARI** depends on `k` and on the labels: the eight labels are not equally
  separable, and the two partitions have different numbers of groups (12 vs. 8).
  Compare ARI only at a fixed `k`.
* **Node purity** rises with the number of nodes; compare it only at a fixed
  grid size.
* **Ambiguity** ratios of different distance functions are not strictly
  comparable. Compare levels *within* one distance only.
* **`ari_node_majority`** (computed in the run engine) labels every node with
  its majority population and scores that. It does not involve the metaclustering
  step, so it shows whether a change in `ari` comes from the SOM or from the
  consensus step.

**Reference value for `ari_donor`.** Donors differ in composition, so even a
*perfect* clustering has a non-zero ARI against donor:

```{r donor-floor-ref}
donor_floor <- ari_score(pop, donor)
cat("ARI(population, donor) =", round(donor_floor, 4), "\n")
```

`ari_donor` is therefore read against `donor_floor` = `r round(donor_floor, 3)`,
not against 0. Values clearly *above* it indicate a clustering that splits
populations by donor. Values *below* it are not automatically "better": they can
also mean the population structure is lost (as at very large cofactors in stage
0).

## Diagnostics: do the markers need scaling?

Before any clustering we look at the data. The diagnostics answer four
questions, in this order, and end with concrete expectations for the factorial:

1. What does the SOM actually "see": which marker gets how much weight?
2. Are donor offsets technical (batch) or compositional (different cell mixes)?
3. Is a marker's spread (its weight) a good proxy for its information?
4. Where does the summary statistic used for (3), eta^2, mislead?

All plots use the paper cofactors.

### What the SOM sees: SD, mean and weight per marker

Euclidean-type distances are translation-invariant per marker (shifting a marker
moves all cells equally), so a marker's **mean** has no effect on clustering, but
its **spread** (SD) sets its weight: in a squared Euclidean distance a marker
contributes in proportion to its variance. Because arcsinh turns absolute
differences at high intensity into fold changes, a transformed-space difference
is already a relative difference where relative differences are meaningful. The
spread is therefore *not* arbitrary, but it is also not guaranteed to track
biology (it also depends on the cofactor, noise and sample composition). Steps
2 and 3 below measure this directly.

The "paper" cofactors are the reference transform for all diagnostics. They are
also reused by the cofactor factor and by several checks later on.

```{r paper-cofactors}
spectral_cofactors <- setNames(rep(6000, length(all_m)), all_m)
spectral_cofactors[c("CD14", "CD19", "CD3", "CD56", "CD45RA", "CD8", "CD4", "CCR7")] <-
    c(10000, 1000, 3000, 2000, 4000, 3000, 5000, 6000)
E_paper <- asinh(sweep(raw[, type_m], 2, spectral_cofactors[type_m], "/"))

marker_ranges <- t(apply(E_paper, 2, function(v)
    c(min = min(v), max = max(v), mean = mean(v), sd = sd(v))))
marker_ranges <- as.data.frame(round(marker_ranges, 2))
marker_ranges[order(-marker_ranges$sd), ]
```

The 13 type markers fall into two groups. Eight have SD between about 0.8 and
1.6 (CD19, CD8, CD3, CD4, CD45RA, CD56, HLA-DR, CCR7). Five have SD of 0.4 or
less (CD16, CD95, GNLY, CD14, CD103). In an unscaled SOM the first group
carries nearly all the weight. Whether that is the right split is the question
of the next steps.

Per-donor view. The first plot shows the SD of each marker within each donor.

```{r per-sample-stats}
#' Per-group mean and SD for every column, computed with rowsum() (vectorised).
group_stats <- function(E, group) {
    s1 <- rowsum(E, group); s2 <- rowsum(E^2, group)
    n  <- as.numeric(table(group)[rownames(s1)])
    mu <- s1 / n
    sdv <- sqrt(pmax(s2 - n * mu^2, 0) / (n - 1))
    long <- function(M, nm) {
        d <- as.data.frame(as.table(M), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
        names(d) <- c("sample_id", "marker", nm); d
    }
    merge(long(mu, "mean"), long(sdv, "sd"))
}
per_sample <- group_stats(E_paper, donor_lab)
marker_order <- names(sort(tapply(per_sample$sd, per_sample$marker, median), decreasing = TRUE))
per_sample$marker <- factor(per_sample$marker, levels = marker_order)
```

```{r fig-per-sample-sd, fig.width = 9}
p <- ggplot(per_sample, aes(marker, sd)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") +
    geom_jitter(aes(colour = sample_id), width = 0.15, size = 2) +
    labs(x = "Type marker", y = "Per-sample SD", colour = "Sample",
         title = "Per-sample SD of arcsinh-transformed expression") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
show_plot(p, "diag_per_sample_sd", 9, 5)
```

The marker ranking by SD is the same in every donor, so the weight structure is
a property of the panel, not of individual donors. The markers with the widest
per-donor ranges (CD19, CD8, CD56, CCR7, CD16) are the ones whose positive
fraction varies between donors. For a bimodal marker the SD depends on the
proportion of positive cells (it is largest at 50:50), so these ranges are
partly a composition signal.

The second plot shows the per-donor means.

```{r fig-per-sample-mean, fig.width = 9}
p <- ggplot(per_sample, aes(marker, mean)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "grey90") +
    geom_jitter(aes(colour = sample_id), width = 0.15, size = 2) +
    labs(x = "Type marker", y = "Per-sample mean", colour = "Sample",
         title = "Per-sample mean of arcsinh-transformed expression") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
show_plot(p, "diag_per_sample_mean", 9, 5)
```

Donor offsets are each donor's mean minus the marker's mean across donors. A
shift here is exactly what a per-donor centring (`donor_median`, `donor_z`) would
remove.

```{r fig-donor-offsets, fig.width = 9}
per_sample$offset <- per_sample$mean - ave(per_sample$mean, per_sample$marker)
p <- ggplot(per_sample, aes(marker, offset, colour = sample_id)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 2) +
    labs(x = "Type marker", y = "Donor mean minus mean across donors", colour = "Sample",
         title = "Donor offsets in mean expression (confounded with composition)") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
show_plot(p, "diag_donor_offsets", 9, 5)
```

Most offsets are within about +/-0.5 arcsinh units, but several donor means for
bright, bimodal markers (CD3, CD45RA, CD4) sit far from the rest. The plot title
says why this cannot be read at face value: a donor with few T cells has a low
CD3 mean without any technical difference. The next step separates the two
explanations.

### Are the donor offsets technical or compositional?

Each donor has a different mix of populations, so a shifted donor mean may
simply mean "more T cells". The clean test is **within a known population**: for
each population x marker, how much do the per-donor means differ? If the cell
type is held fixed, composition cannot explain the difference. Values are in
arcsinh units (about natural-log units for bright cells, so 0.3 is roughly a
1.35-fold shift).

```{r fig-within-pop-donor-sd, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
rs <- rowsum(E_paper, paste(pop, donor_lab, sep = "|"))
mu_pd <- rs / as.numeric(table(paste(pop, donor_lab, sep = "|"))[rownames(rs)])
pop_of_row <- sub("\\|.*", "", rownames(mu_pd))
donor_sd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(seq_len(nrow(mu_pd)), pop_of_row),
                                  function(i) apply(mu_pd[i, , drop = FALSE], 2, sd)))
d <- as.data.frame(as.table(donor_sd), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
names(d) <- c("population", "marker", "sd_across_donors")
p <- ggplot(d, aes(marker, population, fill = sd_across_donors)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", sd_across_donors)), size = 2.5) +
    scale_fill_viridis(name = "SD of donor\nmeans") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL,
         title = "Between-donor SD of within-population means (technical offset)") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
                            panel.grid = element_blank())
show_plot(p, "diag_within_population_donor_sd", 9, 4.5)
```

```{r donor-sd-summary}
ccr7_sd   <- donor_sd[, "CCR7"]
other_sd  <- donor_sd[, colnames(donor_sd) != "CCR7"]
med_other <- median(other_sd)
```

Reading the heatmap:

* **CCR7 is the one channel that is elevated in every population.** Its
  between-donor SD ranges from `r round(min(ccr7_sd), 2)` to
  `r round(max(ccr7_sd), 2)` (median `r round(median(ccr7_sd), 2)`), against a
  median of `r round(med_other, 2)` for all other marker x population
  combinations. The largest values are in the naive subsets (naive CD8+:
  `r round(donor_sd["Naive_CD8+_T_cells", "CCR7"], 2)`; naive CD4+:
  `r round(donor_sd["Naive_CD4+_T_cells", "CCR7"], 2)`). These populations are
  gated as CCR7+, so a shift this large *within* an already-positive population
  cannot be composition. A channel-wide effect, rather than a population-specific
  one, points to the measurement itself: CCR7 sits on a different fluorophore in
  donors 5-7 (see the swap above), and donor- or batch-dependent
  staining/titration is the other candidate.
* **CD56 shows a population-specific pattern**, concentrated in the TEMRA
  compartment (TEMRA CD8+: `r round(donor_sd["TEMRA_CD8+_T_cells", "CD56"], 2)`,
  the largest value in the matrix; TEMRA CD4+:
  `r round(donor_sd["TEMRA_CD4+_T_cells", "CD56"], 2)`). CD56 is a dim,
  low-expression marker on T cells, so this more plausibly reflects genuine
  donor-to-donor biological variability in CD56+ "NKT-like" content, amplified by
  the marker's low dynamic range. This is an interpretation; the data do not
  distinguish the two.
* **Secondary offsets** appear for CD16 in NK cells
  (`r round(donor_sd["NK_cells", "CD16"], 2)`) and for CD45RA in several
  populations (for example TEMRA CD8+:
  `r round(donor_sd["TEMRA_CD8+_T_cells", "CD45RA"], 2)`).
* **Everything else is mostly small**: the median over the other combinations is
  `r round(med_other, 2)`, with a handful of values between 0.35 and 0.5.

The swap makes CCR7 the natural test case. If the within-population offset
follows the fluorophore assignment, donors 5-7 should separate from donors 1-4:

```{r fig-ccr7-by-donor, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4}
naive_rows <- grepl("^Naive_", rownames(mu_pd))
ccr7_naive <- data.frame(
    population = sub("\\|.*", "", rownames(mu_pd))[naive_rows],
    donor = sub(".*\\|", "", rownames(mu_pd))[naive_rows],
    ccr7 = mu_pd[naive_rows, "CCR7"])
ccr7_naive$fluorophore <- ifelse(ccr7_naive$donor %in% paste0("donor", 5:7),
                                 "donors 5-7: CCR7 on AF488", "donors 1-4: CCR7 on AF700")
grp_mean <- tapply(ccr7_naive$ccr7, ccr7_naive$fluorophore, mean)
p <- ggplot(ccr7_naive, aes(donor, ccr7, colour = fluorophore, shape = population)) +
    geom_point(size = 3) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Mean CCR7 (arcsinh) within the population",
         colour = NULL, shape = NULL,
         title = "CCR7 within naive T cells, by donor and fluorophore") +
    theme_minimal()
show_plot(p, "diag_ccr7_by_donor", 8, 4)
```

The group means within naive T cells are
`r round(grp_mean[["donors 1-4: CCR7 on AF700"]], 2)` (donors 1-4, AF700) and
`r round(grp_mean[["donors 5-7: CCR7 on AF488"]], 2)` (donors 5-7, AF488), a
difference of
`r round(grp_mean[["donors 5-7: CCR7 on AF488"]] - grp_mean[["donors 1-4: CCR7 on AF700"]], 2)`
arcsinh units, to be compared with the between-donor SD above. A group
difference of that order means the CCR7 offset is technical and tied to the
fluorophore; a small one means it is donor-to-donor variation within each group.
With three and four donors per group this is a check, not a test.

This also fixes how the donor-based scalings should be judged later. Per-donor
*centring* has a legitimate target only where offsets are technical, and that is
a minority of marker x population combinations (CCR7 mainly). Everywhere else a
donor-wise statistic carries composition.

### Is a marker's SD a good proxy for its importance?

Imagine the SOM is sorting cells into groups by measuring how "different" they
look from each other, marker by marker. If one marker's numbers swing wildly
across cells (a big spread, i.e. a high standard deviation, or SD) while another
marker's numbers barely move, the SOM will pay far more attention to the first
marker without being told to: it just naturally dominates the "distance"
calculation because its values are bigger and more spread out, like one really
loud voice in a group conversation drowning out quieter ones. The problem is that
a marker can be loud (high SD) without being useful: it might vary a lot just
because of staining differences between donors or machine noise, not because it
actually distinguishes one cell type from another. Conversely, a marker can be
quiet (low SD) but still be exactly what you need to tell two cell types apart,
if that marker is the one thing those two types truly differ on. So SD alone
tells you how much weight a marker gets in clustering, not whether that weight is
earned. To check whether it is earned, you need a second measure, eta^2, that
asks "how much of this marker's variation actually lines up with real, known
differences between cell types?" rather than just "how much does this marker vary
overall?"

#### What is eta^2, exactly?

eta^2 ("eta squared") is a number between 0 and 1 that answers one specific
question: "if I only knew which of the 8 known cell populations a cell belongs
to, how much of that marker's total variation could I explain just from the
population label?" The code computes it the classic one-way-ANOVA way: split all
the cells into their population groups, see how far each group's *average* for
that marker is from the overall average (this is the "between-group" variation,
the part explained by population identity), and compare that to how much the
marker varies in total, including the spread of individual cells *within* each
population (this is the "total" variation, which = between-group variation +
within-group noise). eta^2 = between-group variation / total variation.

* **eta^2 close to 1** means: almost all of this marker's variation is "between
  populations". Cells within the same population have nearly the same value, but
  different populations have very different values. That is the signature of a
  marker that cleanly separates cell types (e.g. CD19 for B cells: B cells are
  uniformly high, everything else is uniformly low).
* **eta^2 close to 0** means: this marker's variation has almost nothing to do
  with which population a cell is in. Cells scatter just as much *within* a
  single population as they do *across* different populations. That can happen
  for two different reasons: either the marker carries no real biological
  information for distinguishing these populations (CD45 is the extreme case
  of this -- high on every leukocyte, so it cannot tell populations apart --
  which is exactly why it is excluded from the SOM features above rather than
  merely down-weighted), or it carries
  information the 8 fixed population labels don't capture well, for example a
  marker that tracks a continuous, graded process like differentiation stage
  rather than a sharp category, so cells within the same labeled population can
  still differ a lot on it (this is closer to what is happening with CCR7).

The reason eta^2 is the right partner for SD is that SD only measures "how much
does this marker move overall", while eta^2 measures "how much of that movement
is actually meaningful (population-aligned)" rather than noise, donor
variability, or continuous biological drift that the discrete population labels
don't capture. Note that eta^2 uses the labels: it is a diagnostic, never an
input to an unsupervised pipeline.

```{r marker-info}
marker_info <- data.frame(sd = apply(E_paper, 2, sd), eta2 = eta2(E_paper, pop))
marker_info[order(-marker_info$eta2), ]
```

To look for biological patterns in where markers fall, each marker is coloured
by a **biological prior** defined *before* looking at the plot: its behaviour
along the naive -> effector/memory differentiation axis. The colour must not be
adjusted to make the pattern neat, otherwise it would only restate the plot.

* `down`: lost upon differentiation (CCR7, CD45RA).
* `up`: gained with an effector/cytotoxic/memory phenotype (CD95, CD56, GNLY,
  HLA-DR).
* `lineage`: subset-defining markers that are not regulated by differentiation
  state per se (CD3, CD4, CD8, CD19, CD14, CD16, CD103). CD16 belongs here:
  across these eight populations its main source of variance is NK cells vs.
  everyone else, a lineage role, not a graded differentiation state.

```{r fig-eta2, fig.width = 8}
marker_info$regulation <- factor(
    ifelse(rownames(marker_info) %in% c("CCR7", "CD45RA"), "down",
    ifelse(rownames(marker_info) %in% c("CD95", "CD56", "GNLY", "HLA-DR"), "up",
           "lineage")),
    levels = c("up", "down", "lineage"))

p <- ggplot(marker_info, aes(sd, eta2, label = rownames(marker_info),
                              colour = regulation)) +
    geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed",
                colour = "grey70") +
    geom_point(size = 2.5) +
    { if (requireNamespace("ggrepel", quietly = TRUE))
          ggrepel::geom_text_repel(show.legend = FALSE)
      else geom_text(vjust = -0.6, show.legend = FALSE) } +
    scale_colour_manual(
        name = "Differentiation\ndirection",
        values = c(up = "firebrick", down = "steelblue", lineage = "grey40"),
        labels = c(up = "Up with differentiation",
                   down = "Down with differentiation",
                   lineage = "Lineage marker")) +
    labs(x = "Total SD (sets the marker's weight in the unscaled SOM distance)",
         y = "Fraction of variance explained by known population (eta^2)",
         title = "Marker SD vs. marker information") +
    theme_minimal()
show_plot(p, "diag_sd_vs_eta2", 8, 5)
```

**Reading the plot.** The dashed line is eta^2 = SD. The two axes have different
units (a fraction vs. arcsinh units), so the line is a visual guide, not a
calibrated target. What counts is the comparison between markers: markers with
high eta^2 but low SD are candidates for up-weighting, and markers with high SD
but low eta^2 are candidates for down-weighting.

* **Seven markers have both high SD and high eta^2** (CD4, CD19, CD3, HLA-DR,
  CD8, CD45RA, CD56; SD 1.0-1.6, eta^2 0.77-0.97). They fall below the dashed
  line only because eta^2 is bounded at 1 while SD is not (a ceiling effect, not
  a problem): they get high SOM weight *and* carry high information, which is
  what you want.
* **CD95 and CD16 carry more information than their modest SD suggests**
  (SD `r round(marker_info["CD95", "sd"], 2)` and
  `r round(marker_info["CD16", "sd"], 2)`; eta^2
  `r round(marker_info["CD95", "eta2"], 2)` and
  `r round(marker_info["CD16", "eta2"], 2)`). They sit above or on the line, and
  are the natural candidates for up-weighting.
* **CD103, CD14 and GNLY carry little information and little weight** (SD
  0.20-0.34, eta^2 at most `r round(max(marker_info[c("CD103", "CD14", "GNLY"), "eta2"]), 2)`).
  This is expected for CD14, a myeloid marker that is absent from these
  lymphocyte populations (CD45 would belong in this group too -- every subset
  is CD45+, so it cannot discriminate between them -- which is why it is
  excluded from the SOM features entirely rather than left in to be
  down-weighted). Their low SD keeps them quiet in the unscaled SOM. This
  is the group that z-scoring would inflate to SD = 1, which is the basis of H1.
* **CCR7 is the exception among the high-SD markers.** At SD
  `r round(marker_info["CCR7", "sd"], 2)` its variance is
  `r round(marker_info["CCR7", "sd"]^2 / marker_info["HLA-DR", "sd"]^2, 2)` times
  that of HLA-DR, which sets its weight in a squared distance. Yet its eta^2 is
  only `r round(marker_info["CCR7", "eta2"], 2)`, a gap that the ceiling effect
  cannot explain. This is consistent with CCR7 being lost gradually along the
  differentiation trajectory rather than marking a discrete population boundary.
  It also matches the previous step: CCR7 has the largest between-donor offsets
  within populations, so part of its within-population spread is donor noise
  rather than biology.

So CCR7 looks like the strongest candidate for scaling or down-weighting. Whether
its weight actually *hurts* the clustering is a different question, which eta^2
cannot answer.

### A blind spot in eta^2

eta^2 is a *retrospective, aggregate* statistic: it uses the true labels to ask,
averaged across all 8 populations at once, how much of a marker's variance lines
up with population identity. What it cannot tell you is whether that marker
creates risk for a *specific* cell in a *specific* pairwise confusion. A marker
can have a respectable overall eta^2, driven by the fact that it cleanly
separates most population pairs, while still being exactly the marker that, for
one particular cell, outweighs the correct signal from every other marker and
pulls that cell's raw, unscaled distance closer to the wrong population's
centroid than to its own. eta^2 averages this risk away because it is a summary
over the whole dataset. The unscaled SOM, by contrast, makes its routing decision
per cell, in the full multi-marker distance space, where one high-SD/low-eta^2
marker (CCR7, say) could dominate a single cell's distance even though its
*average* behaviour looks only moderate.

The diagnostic below replaces the question "does this marker separate
populations on average" with "for cells that would actually be mis-routed in
unscaled distance space, which marker is responsible". For every cell it compares
the squared distance to its own population's centroid with the distance to the
nearest *other* centroid. A cell closer to a wrong centroid is at risk of being
mis-routed. For those cells only, the squared-distance gap is split by marker.

```{r fig-marker-pull-contamination, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5}
pop_f <- factor(pop)
centroids <- rowsum(E_paper, pop_f) / as.numeric(table(pop_f))
centroids <- centroids[levels(pop_f), , drop = FALSE]

own_c <- centroids[as.integer(pop_f), , drop = FALSE]
d_own <- rowSums((E_paper - own_c)^2)

dist_all <- vapply(rownames(centroids), function(p) {
    rowSums(sweep(E_paper, 2, centroids[p, ], "-")^2)
}, numeric(nrow(E_paper)))
dist_all[cbind(seq_len(nrow(dist_all)), as.integer(pop_f))] <- Inf

nearest_wrong <- max.col(-dist_all, ties.method = "first")
d_wrong <- dist_all[cbind(seq_len(nrow(dist_all)), nearest_wrong)]
wrong_pop <- rownames(centroids)[nearest_wrong]

misassigned <- d_wrong < d_own
cat(sprintf("%.1f%% of cells sit closer, in raw unscaled distance, to a wrong population centroid than to their own.\n",
            100 * mean(misassigned)))

## Decompose the distance gap by marker, for misassigned cells only.
mi <- which(misassigned)
x        <- E_paper[mi, , drop = FALSE]
own_mu   <- centroids[as.integer(pop_f[mi]), , drop = FALSE]
wrong_mu <- centroids[wrong_pop[mi], , drop = FALSE]

## positive = this marker pushes the cell toward the WRONG centroid
pull <- (x - own_mu)^2 - (x - wrong_mu)^2
pull_summary <- sort(colMeans(pull), decreasing = TRUE)

d <- data.frame(marker = factor(names(pull_summary), levels = rev(names(pull_summary))),
                pull = pull_summary)
p <- ggplot(d, aes(pull, marker)) +
    geom_col(fill = "firebrick") +
    labs(x = "Mean per-marker contribution to the wrong-centroid pull\n(misassigned cells only, raw units)",
         y = NULL,
         title = "Which markers drive cell-level mis-routing risk") +
    theme_minimal()
show_plot(p, "diag_marker_pull_contamination", 8, 4.5)
```

Where those at-risk cells come from, and which populations they are pulled
towards:

```{r pull-tables}
## share of each population's cells that is closer to a wrong centroid
sort(round(100 * tapply(misassigned, pop_f, mean), 1), decreasing = TRUE)
## own population (rows) vs. nearest wrong population (columns), at-risk cells only
table(own = pop_f[mi], nearest_wrong = wrong_pop[mi])
```

**Result.** Only `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean(misassigned))`% of cells lie closer
to a wrong centroid, so the unscaled metric routes the large majority correctly.
For the at-risk cells the pull is dominated by **CD56**
(`r sprintf("%.2f", pull_summary[["CD56"]])`), followed by **CD8**
(`r sprintf("%.2f", pull_summary[["CD8"]])`). **CCR7 does not drive
mis-routing: its contribution is negative**
(`r sprintf("%.2f", pull_summary[["CCR7"]])`), i.e. on these cells it pulls
towards their *own* centroid. CCR7's low eta^2 therefore reflects within-population
spread of a graded marker, not routing risk.

CD56 and CD8 are high-eta^2 markers (`r round(marker_info["CD56", "eta2"], 2)` and
`r round(marker_info["CD8", "eta2"], 2)`), so their pull comes from large
within-population spread relative to the gap between neighbouring populations,
exactly the situation the blind-spot paragraph describes. For CD56 this fits the
dim, variable expression on T cells noted in the donor-offset step. The tables
above show which population pairs are involved.

Two limits apply. A nearest-centroid rule treats each population as a single
blob, whereas some populations form a continuum (naive -> memory -> TEMRA), so it
is a crude proxy for what a 100-node SOM does. And the diagnostic uses the
labels, so it explains but cannot be used for correction.

### What the diagnostics imply for the factors

These are **expectations**, to be tested by the factorial and not conclusions.

* **Unscaled data already weight roughly by information.** The markers with the
  largest SD are, with the exception of CCR7, the markers with the highest eta^2,
  and the markers with almost no information (CD14, GNLY, CD103) have the
  smallest SD. Rescaling every marker to the same spread would give these noise
  markers the same weight as CD3 or CD19. This is the reasoning behind **H1**.
* **CCR7's weight is not the problem it first appears to be.** It combines high
  SD, low eta^2 and the largest technical offsets, which makes it the obvious
  candidate for down-weighting, but the cell-level diagnostic shows that it does
  not drive mis-routing. Oracle weights (**H5**) will show how much is at stake in
  the weights overall.
* **Donor offsets are mostly compositional, with one technical exception.**
  Within a population most between-donor differences are small, with CCR7 (and to
  a lesser degree CD56) as exceptions. A donor-wise centring (`donor_median`,
  `donor_z`) or a correction that treats each donor as a batch (cyCombine) removes
  the technical part but also the composition signal, which is the logic behind
  **H2** and **H4**.
* **Spread is a property of the panel.** The SD ranking is the same in every
  donor, so differences between scalings are not an artefact of a few donors.
  

## Implementing the factors

Every cell of the factorial is the composition
`cofactor -> (batch correction) -> scaling -> weighting -> distance`. Each factor
below is a small function. For each one: what it does, what we expect, and what
could make it misleading.

### Factor 1: arcsinh cofactor strategies

`arcsinh(x / c)` is ~linear for x << c and ~logarithmic for x >> c, so the
cofactor `c` sets where on the raw intensity scale the switch happens. Too small:
near-zero noise is stretched and dim populations smear. Too large: everything is
linear and the brightest markers dominate. Stage 0 maps this out for flat
cofactors.

* `paper`: hand-tuned per-marker cofactors from Tursi et al. 2025 (eight lineage
  markers), with 6,000 (CytoPheno's spectral default) for the other 16.
* `flat_<value>`: one cofactor for all markers. `flat_150` is the conventional
  flow default and is expected to do badly on spectral data (negative control);
  `flat_6000` is the spectral default; `flat_<best>` is the best flat value from
  stage 0 (**oracle**, chosen by mean ARI over seeds).
* `cyet_donor`: CyEt estimates, **per donor and per marker**, the cofactor
  `b = 1.1^k` that makes the windowed marker distribution most Gaussian
  (Shapiro-Wilk). Fully label-free, but it optimises normality, not
  separability, and a per-donor transform can itself create donor differences.
  This requires `support/cyet/cyet_per_donor_resolved.rds`.

  *Regenerated 2026-10-25 with CyEt 0.99.13* (up from 0.99.12), which added
  adaptive range extension and explicit convergence status
  (`"converged"`/`"boundary"`/`"non_convergent"`) to `optimizeBvalueVector()`.
  Of the 168 donor x marker fits, only CD45 failed to converge (5 of 7
  donors), and only because CD45 genuinely has no negative population in
  this dataset to make Gaussian (see the SOM-markers section above) -- the
  new adaptive range widening correctly exhausted itself rather than
  fabricating a spurious optimum. Non-converged donors are resolved per
  marker with `detect_bimodal_split()`: toward the nearest cluster's median
  when the converged donors' own b-values split into two groups, otherwise
  toward their pooled median (CD45's case: only 2 donors converged, so no
  split test was possible; all 5 failed donors used the pooled median of
  those 2, 241,557). This replaced the previous version's unconditional
  replace-with-global-median, which is exactly the failure mode flagged in
  `CyEt.compare`'s improvement-plan document for a training set that itself
  splits bimodally.

Cofactors are stored either as a **named vector** (one value per marker, shared
by all donors) or as a **donors x markers matrix** (per-donor).

```{r cofactors}
cof_registry <- list(paper = spectral_cofactors)

cyet_file <- "support/cyet/cyet_per_donor_resolved.rds"
if (file.exists(cyet_file)) {
    pdc <- readRDS(cyet_file)
    ## donor index in that file = position of the donor in unique(sce$donor), i.e. donor1..donor7
    cyet_mat <- matrix(NA_real_, 7, length(all_m), dimnames = list(1:7, all_m))
    cyet_mat[cbind(pdc$donor, match(pdc$marker, all_m))] <- pdc$b_resolved
    stopifnot(!anyNA(cyet_mat))
    cof_registry$cyet_donor <- cyet_mat
} else {
    message("No CyEt file at ", cyet_file, "; the cyet_donor cofactor set is skipped.")
}

#' Canonical name for a flat cofactor set, never in scientific notation.
flat_name <- function(x) paste0("flat_", format(x, scientific = FALSE, trim = TRUE))

#' Resolve a cofactor-set name to a named vector (global) or donors x markers matrix.
#' Names of the form "flat_<number>" are created on the fly.
get_cofactors <- function(name) {
    if (!is.null(cof_registry[[name]])) return(cof_registry[[name]])
    if (grepl("^flat_[0-9.]+(e[+-]?[0-9]+)?$", name)) {   # also tolerate "flat_1e+05"
        return(setNames(rep(as.numeric(sub("^flat_", "", name)), length(all_m)), all_m))
    }
    stop("unknown cofactor set: ", name)
}

#' arcsinh-transform the raw matrix (cells x 24) with a cofactor set.
#' Per-donor matrices are applied donor by donor.
transform_raw <- function(cof) {
    out <- raw
    if (is.matrix(cof)) {
        for (d in sort(unique(donor))) {
            j <- which(donor == d)
            out[j, ] <- asinh(sweep(raw[j, , drop = FALSE], 2, cof[as.character(d), all_m], "/"))
        }
    } else {
        out <- asinh(sweep(raw, 2, cof[all_m], "/"))
    }
    out
}
```

### Factor 2: batch correction (cyCombine)

cyCombine (Pedersen et al. 2022) first clusters cells with a small internal SOM
(8x8) and then runs `sva::ComBat` **within each cluster**, so the correction does
not remove between-population differences that are unevenly spread across
batches. Here each donor is a batch. The correction runs on all 24 markers after
the cofactor transform, and the result is cached per cofactor set (it is the most
expensive step: allow tens of minutes per set on 725,000 cells).

Two caveats shape how the result should be read. "Donor = batch" assumes donors
differ technically, not in composition, but the within-population heatmap showed
that most offsets are small. And ComBat is fitted per cluster, so rare
donor x cluster combinations (some donor x population cells have only a few
dozen events, see the table in Data) get unreliable corrections.

```{r cycombine}
#' cyCombine-corrected, arcsinh-transformed matrix (cells x 24) for a cofactor set.
#' Cached on disk; the (slow) correction only runs if the cache file is missing.
correct_cycombine <- function(cf) {
    path <- file.path(out_dir, "cycombine", paste0("cc_", cf, ".rds"))
    if (file.exists(path)) return(readRDS(path))
    message("[cyCombine] correcting cofactor set '", cf, "' (slow) ...")
    df <- as.data.frame(transform_raw(get_cofactors(cf)))
    df$batch <- donor_lab
    df$id <- seq_len(nrow(df))
    set.seed(1234)
    cc <- cyCombine::batch_correct(
        df, markers = all_m, label = NULL,       # label = NULL: cyCombine builds its own internal SOM
        xdim = 8, ydim = 8, seed = 1234,
        norm_method = "scale", method = "ComBat") # "scale" only feeds the grouping SOM
    cc <- as.data.frame(cc)
    cc <- cc[order(cc$id), ]
    out <- as.matrix(cc[, all_m]); rownames(out) <- NULL
    save_rds_atomic(out, path)
    out
}

#' Cells x type-marker matrix after cofactor transform (+ optional cyCombine).
get_base <- function(cf, batch) {
    tr <- if (batch == "cyCombine") correct_cycombine(cf) else transform_raw(get_cofactors(cf))
    tr[, type_m, drop = FALSE]
}
```

### Factor 3: scaling

All methods act on the 13 type markers, after cofactor transform and batch
correction. Centring is irrelevant for Manhattan, Euclidean and Chebyshev, so the
**centering part** only matters for cosine; the **scale part** matters for all
four distances.

| Method | Definition | What it changes | Main risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| `none` | x | reference | CCR7-like high-SD markers carry large weight |
| `center_global` | x - mean | nothing for L1/L2/L-inf (**invariance test**); the origin for cosine | none |
| `donor_median` | x - median of that donor | removes per-donor additive offsets (= multiplicative gain in raw intensity); spread untouched | the median of a bimodal marker depends on the donor's population mix, so it can inject composition |
| `alpha0.5` | (x - mean) / sd^0.5 | partial equalisation of spread (alpha = 0 none, 1 = z-score) | mild |
| `zscore` | (x - mean) / sd | all markers SD = 1 | inflates low-SD (often noise) markers |
| `robust_z` | (x - median) / MAD | like z-score, outlier-robust | inflates even more for markers with most cells near zero (tiny MAD) |
| `pct_range` | (x - q01) / (q99 - q01) | CATALYST's heatmap scaling, 1st-99th percentile to 0-1 | milder than z-score: for Gaussian noise q99 - q01 is ~4.65 SD |
| `donor_z` | per-donor median centering, then divide by the global SD | donor alignment + equalised spread | both risks above |

```{r scaling}
#' Subtract a per-donor statistic (e.g. column medians) from every donor's cells.
center_by_donor <- function(X, fun = matrixStats::colMedians) {
    for (d in unique(donor)) {
        j <- which(donor == d)
        X[j, ] <- sweep(X[j, , drop = FALSE], 2, fun(X[j, , drop = FALSE]), "-")
    }
    X
}

#' Apply a scaling method (see table above) to a cells x markers matrix.
apply_scaling <- function(X, how) {
    switch(how,
        none          = X,
        center_global = sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X), "-"),
        donor_median  = center_by_donor(X),
        alpha0.5      = sweep(sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X), "-"), 2, colSds(X)^0.5, "/"),
        zscore        = sweep(sweep(X, 2, colMeans(X), "-"), 2, colSds(X), "/"),
        robust_z      = sweep(sweep(X, 2, colMedians(X), "-"), 2,
                              pmax(colMads(X), 1e-8), "/"),
        pct_range     = { q <- colQuantiles(X, probs = c(0.01, 0.99))
                          sweep(sweep(X, 2, q[, 1], "-"), 2, q[, 2] - q[, 1], "/") },
        donor_z       = { Xc <- center_by_donor(X); sweep(Xc, 2, colSds(Xc), "/") },
        stop("unknown scaling: ", how))
}
```

### Factor 4: marker weights

`sqrt_eta2` multiplies every marker by the square root of its between-population
variance fraction (so its *variance* is scaled by eta^2). It uses the labels,
hence it is an **oracle**: an upper bound on what any weighting could achieve,
not a method for unlabeled data.

`FlowSOM::SOM()` also has an `importance` argument. For the Euclidean case,
pre-multiplying columns is mathematically equivalent, and it keeps the data and
the code book in the same space for the ambiguity calculation. The check below
tests this for Euclidean.

```{r weights}
apply_weights <- function(X, how) {
    if (how == "none") return(X)
    if (how == "sqrt_eta2") return(sweep(X, 2, sqrt(eta2(X, pop)), "*"))
    stop("unknown weighting: ", how)
}

prepare_X <- function(Xbase, scaling, weighting) {
    apply_weights(apply_scaling(Xbase, scaling), weighting)
}
```

```{r importance-check}
importance_check <- cached("01_importance_check.rds", {
    set.seed(1)
    ii <- sort(sample(N, min(50000, N)))
    Xs <- E_paper[ii, ]
    w  <- sqrt(eta2(Xs, droplevels(pop[ii])))
    set.seed(7); som_imp <- FlowSOM::SOM(Xs, xdim = 10, ydim = 10, importance = w, silent = TRUE)
    set.seed(7); som_pre <- FlowSOM::SOM(sweep(Xs, 2, w, "*"), xdim = 10, ydim = 10, silent = TRUE)
    node <- as.integer(som_imp$mapping[, 1])
    occ <- sort(unique(node))
    node_mean <- function(M) rowsum(M, node) / as.numeric(table(node)[as.character(occ)])
    rmse <- function(a, b) sqrt(mean((a - b)^2))
    data.frame(
        rmse_codes_vs_unweighted_node_means = rmse(som_imp$codes[occ, ], node_mean(Xs)),
        rmse_codes_vs_weighted_node_means   = rmse(som_imp$codes[occ, ], node_mean(sweep(Xs, 2, w, "*"))),
        ari_nodes_importance_vs_premultiplied =
            ari_score(node, as.integer(som_pre$mapping[, 1])))
})
importance_check
```

The code book is much closer to the *weighted* node means (RMSE
`r signif(importance_check[[2]], 3)`) than to the unweighted ones
(`r signif(importance_check[[1]], 3)`), and the node assignments of the two runs
agree (ARI = `r signif(importance_check[[3]], 3)`). For Euclidean,
pre-multiplication is therefore a safe stand-in for `importance=`. For the other
three distances it simply *defines* the weighted distance; it was not compared
against `importance=`.

### Factor 5: distance function inside the SOM

| `distf` | Distance | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Manhattan | less dominated by a single large marker difference than Euclidean |
| 2 | Euclidean | FlowSOM / CATALYST default |
| 3 | Chebyshev | only the single largest marker difference counts |
| 4 | cosine | compares **direction**, ignores the overall magnitude of a cell's profile; origin-dependent, so centering and scaling can matter here, unlike for the other three |

The SOM's metaclustering step (`metaClustering_consensus`) always uses Euclidean
hierarchical clustering on the code vectors, regardless of `distf`. Learning rate
and radius use FlowSOM's defaults for all four distances. Non-Euclidean runs are
therefore best read as exploratory. Finally, the engine below assigns cells to
nodes **itself**, under the training distance, instead of trusting
`som$mapping`; the engine checks show why.

## The run engine

`run_one()` performs a single configuration: prepare the matrix, train the SOM
with `FlowSOM::SOM()` directly, assign every cell to its nearest code vector
under the training distance (`assign_nodes()`), consensus-metacluster the code
vectors into `k` groups, map back to cells, and score. Each run writes its own
result file; `run_stage()` skips runs whose file exists and groups the remaining
runs by (cofactor, batch) so each expensive base matrix is built only once and
then shared (forked, copy-on-write) with the parallel workers.

Besides `ari` (metaclusters vs. population), every run records `ari_node_majority`:
the ARI obtained if every SOM node is labelled with its majority population. It
does not depend on the metaclustering step, so it separates SOM quality from
metaclustering luck.

```{r engine}
cfg_cols  <- c("cofactor", "batch", "scaling", "weighting", "distf")
run_cols  <- c(cfg_cols, "seed", "xdim", "k")
n_seeds   <- if (is.null(params$n_seeds)) 5L else as.integer(params$n_seeds)
seeds_all <- 1234L + seq_len(n_seeds) - 1L

run_key <- function(g) {
    gsub("[^A-Za-z0-9_.-]", "_", paste(g$cofactor, g$batch, g$scaling, g$weighting,
        paste0("d", g$distf), paste0("s", g$seed), paste0("g", g$xdim), paste0("k", g$k),
        sep = "__"))
}

#' Nearest SOM node for every cell under distance `distf`, in chunks (memory).
#' Euclidean uses the cross-product identity (only the arg-min is needed).
assign_nodes <- function(X, codes, distf, chunk = 50000L) {
    n <- nrow(X); node <- integer(n)
    for (s in seq(1L, n, by = chunk)) {
        i  <- s:min(s + chunk - 1L, n)
        Xi <- X[i, , drop = FALSE]
        D <- if (distf == 2) {
            outer(rowSums(Xi^2), rowSums(codes^2), "+") - 2 * tcrossprod(Xi, codes)
        } else node_distances(Xi, codes, distf)
        node[i] <- max.col(-D, ties.method = "first")
    }
    node
}

#' Run one configuration.
#' @param Xbase cells x type-markers after cofactor (+ cyCombine)
#' @param cfg one-row data.frame with the columns in `run_cols`
#' @return one-row data.frame: configuration + metrics (see Overview).
#'   `pct_mapping_agree` = agreement of FlowSOM's own `mapping` with our assignment.
#'   Errors are caught and reported in the `error` column instead of aborting the stage.
run_one <- function(Xbase, cfg) {
    t0 <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]]
    out <- data.frame(cfg[, run_cols], ari = NA_real_, ari_node_majority = NA_real_,
        ari_donor = NA_real_, node_purity = NA_real_, pct_ambiguous = NA_real_,
        median_ratio = NA_real_, pct_mapping_agree = NA_real_, n_empty_nodes = NA_integer_,
        runtime_s = NA_real_, error = NA_character_, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
    rownames(out) <- NULL
    tryCatch({
        X <- prepare_X(Xbase, cfg$scaling, cfg$weighting)
        set.seed(cfg$seed)
        som <- FlowSOM::SOM(X, xdim = cfg$xdim, ydim = cfg$xdim, rlen = 10, mst = 1,
                            distf = cfg$distf, silent = TRUE)
        stopifnot(!is.null(som$mapping))
        node <- assign_nodes(X, som$codes, cfg$distf)
        meta <- meta_cluster(som$codes, cfg$k, cfg$seed)
        cl   <- meta[node]
        maj  <- apply(table(node, pop), 1, which.max)       # majority population per node
        out$ari               <- ari_score(cl, pop)
        out$ari_node_majority <- ari_score(maj[as.character(node)], as.integer(pop))
        out$ari_donor         <- ari_score(cl, donor)
        out$node_purity       <- node_purity(node, pop)
        out$n_empty_nodes     <- nrow(som$codes) - length(unique(node))
        amb <- ambiguity_metrics(X, som$codes, node, cfg$distf, amb_idx)
        out$pct_ambiguous     <- amb$pct_ambiguous
        out$median_ratio      <- amb$median_ratio
        out$pct_mapping_agree <- 100 * mean(as.integer(som$mapping[, 1]) == node)
    }, error = function(e) out$error <<- conditionMessage(e))
    out$runtime_s <- proc.time()[["elapsed"]] - t0
    out
}

#' Run (or resume) a stage. Returns all runs of `grid`, cached or fresh.
run_stage <- function(grid, stage) {
    stopifnot(all(run_cols %in% names(grid)))
    dir <- file.path(out_dir, "runs", stage)
    dir.create(dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
    grid$file <- file.path(dir, paste0(run_key(grid), ".rds"))
    todo <- which(!file.exists(grid$file))
    message(sprintf("[%s] %d runs: %d cached, %d to compute (%d core(s))",
        stage, nrow(grid), nrow(grid) - length(todo), length(todo), n_cores))
    groups <- split(todo, paste(grid$cofactor[todo], grid$batch[todo], sep = "||"))
    for (g in names(groups)) {
        rows <- groups[[g]]
        message(sprintf("[%s] base matrix '%s': %d runs", stage, g, length(rows)))
        Xbase <- get_base(grid$cofactor[rows[1]], grid$batch[rows[1]])
        worker <- function(i) {
            res <- run_one(Xbase, grid[i, ])
            save_rds_atomic(res, grid$file[i])
            invisible(NULL)
        }
        invisible(parallel::mclapply(rows, worker, mc.cores = n_cores, mc.preschedule = FALSE))
        rm(Xbase); invisible(gc())
    }
    res <- lapply(grid$file, function(f) if (file.exists(f)) readRDS(f) else NULL)
    if (any(vapply(res, is.null, NA))) {
        warning(sum(vapply(res, is.null, NA)), " run(s) produced no result file ",
                "(worker died, e.g. out of memory). Re-run the chunk to retry them.")
    }
    res <- do.call(rbind, res)
    res$distance <- factor(dist_labels[as.character(res$distf)],
                           levels = unname(dist_labels)[c(2, 1, 3, 4)])
    rownames(res) <- NULL
    res
}
```

## Engine checks (before any stage)

Two cheap, deterministic checks on a 20,000-cell subsample. They isolate the
*mathematics* from the *training noise* that the full runs add.

1. **Translation invariance (H0).** Assign cells to nodes with the original and
   the globally centred data (and centred code book). For Manhattan, Euclidean
   and Chebyshev the assignment must be identical (up to exact ties); for cosine
   it should not be.
2. **Which distance does `som$mapping` use?** Compare FlowSOM's own node mapping
   for a SOM trained with each `distf` against our nearest-node assignment under
   (a) the training distance and (b) Euclidean.

```{r engine-checks}
engine_checks <- cached("01_engine_checks_v2.rds", local({
    set.seed(2)
    ii <- sort(sample(N, min(20000, N)))
    Xs <- E_paper[ii, ]
    mu <- colMeans(Xs)
    do.call(rbind, lapply(1:4, function(d) {
        set.seed(11)
        som <- FlowSOM::SOM(Xs, xdim = 10, ydim = 10, rlen = 10, mst = 1, distf = d, silent = TRUE)
        som_node <- as.integer(som$mapping[, 1])
        own <- assign_nodes(Xs, som$codes, d)
        euc <- assign_nodes(Xs, som$codes, 2)
        ctr <- assign_nodes(sweep(Xs, 2, mu, "-"), sweep(som$codes, 2, mu, "-"), d)
        data.frame(distance = dist_labels[[as.character(d)]],
                   translation_invariant_pct            = 100 * mean(own == ctr),
                   som_mapping_matches_own_distance_pct = 100 * mean(som_node == own),
                   som_mapping_matches_euclidean_pct    = 100 * mean(som_node == euc))
    }))
}))
knitr::kable(engine_checks, digits = 2, format = "pipe")
```

How to read it:

* `translation_invariant_pct` must be ~100 for Manhattan, Euclidean and
  Chebyshev (H0 as a mathematical fact) and may be lower for cosine.
* If `som_mapping_matches_euclidean_pct` is ~100 for **all** distances while
  `som_mapping_matches_own_distance_pct` is not, then `FlowSOM::SOM()` returns a
  Euclidean `mapping` whatever `distf` was used for training. In that case
  `som$mapping` must not be used for non-Euclidean runs: ARI, purity and
  ambiguity would then compare cells and nodes under *different* metrics. This is
  why `run_one()` assigns nodes itself. The column `pct_mapping_agree` in every
  run records how much the two disagree.

**Reference value for `ari_donor`.** Donors differ in composition, so even a
*perfect* clustering has a non-zero ARI against donor:

## Stage 0: flat cofactor sweep

Thirteen flat cofactors, otherwise the baseline (no batch correction, no scaling,
no weights, Euclidean), each with `r n_seeds` seeds (SOM training is stochastic).
The mean over seeds defines the oracle `flat_<best>`.

```{r stage0}
cofactor_grid <- c(50, 100, 150, 250, 500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 6000, 10000, 20000, 50000, 100000)
stage0_grid <- merge(
    data.frame(cofactor = flat_name(cofactor_grid), batch = "none", scaling = "none",
               weighting = "none", distf = 2, xdim = 10, k = 12, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
    data.frame(seed = seeds_all), by = NULL)
stage0_raw <- cached("10_stage0_v2.rds", run_stage(stage0_grid, "stage0_v2"))
stage0_raw$cofactor_value <- as.numeric(sub("^flat_", "", stage0_raw$cofactor))

stage0 <- aggregate(cbind(ari, ari_node_majority, ari_donor, node_purity, pct_ambiguous) ~
                        cofactor_value, stage0_raw, mean)
stage0$ari_sd <- aggregate(ari ~ cofactor_value, stage0_raw, sd)$ari
best_cf <- stage0$cofactor_value[which.max(stage0$ari)]
sd_best <- stage0$ari_sd[which.max(stage0$ari)]; sd_best[is.na(sd_best)] <- 0
plateau <- range(stage0$cofactor_value[stage0$ari >= max(stage0$ari) - max(2 * sd_best, 0.01)])
stage0
```

```{r fig-stage0, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 7}
m_donor <- "ARI vs. donor (dotted = floor of a perfect clustering)"
long0 <- rbind(
    data.frame(cofactor_value = stage0_raw$cofactor_value, metric = "ARI vs. known population", value = stage0_raw$ari),
    data.frame(cofactor_value = stage0_raw$cofactor_value, metric = "Ambiguous cells (%)", value = stage0_raw$pct_ambiguous),
    data.frame(cofactor_value = stage0_raw$cofactor_value, metric = m_donor, value = stage0_raw$ari_donor))
p <- ggplot(long0, aes(cofactor_value, value)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = 1000, xmax = 10000, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#2a9d8f", alpha = 0.08) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 150, colour = "#dc3545", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 6000, colour = "#264653", linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_hline(data = data.frame(metric = m_donor, y = donor_floor), aes(yintercept = y), linetype = "dotted") +
    geom_point(colour = "grey60", alpha = 0.6, size = 1.4) +
    stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "line", colour = "grey30") +
    stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2.5, colour = "#264653") +
    scale_x_log10(breaks = cofactor_grid, labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",")) +
    facet_wrap(~metric, scales = "free_y", ncol = 1) +
    labs(x = "Flat arcsinh cofactor (log scale)", y = NULL,
         title = "Stage 0: flat cofactor sweep (FlowSOM::SOM, Euclidean)",
         subtitle = "Grey: single seeds; dark: mean. Shaded: paper's per-marker range. Red: 150. Dark dashed: 6,000.") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
show_plot(p, "stage0_flat_cofactor_sweep", 8, 7)
```

The best flat cofactor is **`r best_cf`** (mean ARI `r round(max(stage0$ari), 3)`).
All flat values from `r plateau[1]` to `r plateau[2]` lie within two seed-SDs
(minimum 0.01) of it. The flat 6,000 fallback scores
`r round(stage0$ari[stage0$cofactor_value == 6000], 3)` and 150 scores
`r round(stage0$ari[stage0$cofactor_value == 150], 3)`.

How to read this: the ARI curve is a plateau with steep walls. At small cofactors
arcsinh is logarithmic over the whole range and noise around zero is stretched;
at very large cofactors it is linear and the brightest markers dominate. Between
the walls, the exact value hardly matters. That is a prior for the later result
on `paper` (per-marker) vs. flat cofactors. The ambiguity curve is not monotone
with ARI: it peaks inside the plateau, so a better partition can come with more
ambiguous raw nodes. `ari_donor` falls at the largest cofactors only because the
population structure is lost there (compare with the dotted floor).

## Stage 1: the full factorial

```{r stage1-grid}
cof_names <- unique(c("paper", "flat_150", "flat_6000", flat_name(best_cf),
                      if ("cyet_donor" %in% names(cof_registry)) "cyet_donor"))

## cyCombine is slow: apply it to the label-free, sensible cofactor sets only
## (not to the flat_150 negative control).
cc_sets <- setdiff(cof_names, "flat_150")

combos <- data.frame(cofactor = cof_names, batch = "none", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
if (have_cycombine) {
    combos <- rbind(combos, data.frame(cofactor = cc_sets, batch = "cyCombine", stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
}
scalings   <- c("none", "center_global", "donor_median", "alpha0.5", "zscore", "robust_z", "pct_range", "donor_z")
stage1_grid <- merge(combos,
    expand.grid(scaling = scalings, weighting = c("none", "sqrt_eta2"), distf = c(2, 1, 3, 4),
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE), by = NULL)
stage1_grid$seed <- 1234; stage1_grid$xdim <- 10; stage1_grid$k <- 12
cat(nrow(stage1_grid), "stage-1 runs:", nrow(combos), "(cofactor x batch) base matrices x",
    length(scalings), "scalings x 2 weightings x 4 distances\n")
```

### Gating scheme after each cofactor transform, for every cofactor strategy

The same 8-panel gating scheme recreated earlier (per donor, in the Data
section) is repeated here **after the arcsinh transform**, once per entry in
`cof_names` -- i.e. exactly the cofactor strategies this factorial actually
tests (`r paste(cof_names, collapse = ", ")`), so this stays in sync with
whatever `cof_names` resolves to automatically.

Gates 1-2 (the FSC-A/SSC-A lymphocyte and FSC-A/FSC-H singlet gates) are
**not** repeated here: FSC/SSC are scatter channels, never part of the
arcsinh cofactor transform (`all_m` is fluorescence markers only), so those
two panels are identical for every cofactor strategy -- see the versions
already generated above. Only gates 3-8, which plot transformed fluorescence
channels, can actually change with the cofactor choice.

This reuses `raw`/`pop`/`donor`/`all_m` from the Data section and
`get_cofactors()`/`transform_raw()` from "Factor 1" above directly, rather
than re-reading the FCS files -- the transformed matrix for a cofactor set is
exactly what `get_base(cf, "none")` would hand to the clustering stages,
just not yet restricted to `type_m`.

```{r gating-figures-by-method-defs}
gate_defs_post_transform <- Filter(function(g) g$id >= 3, gate_defs)

#' Same plot as gating_make_plot(), but reading x/y directly from an
#' already-transformed cells x markers matrix (no extra display cofactor --
#' `tr` is already asinh(raw / cofactor_set)).
gating_make_plot_transformed <- function(tr, gate, donor_id, method_label) {
    keep <- donor == donor_id & pop %in% gate$pool
    df <- data.frame(x = tr[keep, gate$xcol], y = tr[keep, gate$ycol], population = pop[keep])

    if (is.null(gate$split)) {
        p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y)) +
            geom_hex(bins = 100) +
            scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "turbo", trans = "log10", name = "cells")
    } else if (isTRUE(gate$split$multi)) {
        multi_levels <- c("Naive CD4", "EM CD4", "TEMRA CD4", "Naive CD8", "EM CD8", "TEMRA CD8")
        df$label <- factor(gate_pop_short[as.character(df$population)],
                            levels = intersect(multi_levels, gate_pop_short))
        p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = label)) +
            geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.25) +
            scale_color_brewer(palette = "Set1", name = NULL) +
            guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1)))
    } else {
        df$label <- factor(
            ifelse(as.character(df$population) %in% gate$split$pos, gate$split$label[1], gate$split$label[2]),
            levels = gate$split$label
        )
        p <- ggplot(df, aes(x, y, color = label)) +
            geom_point(size = 0.15, alpha = 0.2) +
            scale_color_manual(values = setNames(c("red3", "grey50"), gate$split$label), name = NULL) +
            guides(color = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2, alpha = 1)))
    }

    p + labs(title = sprintf("%s -- %s", gate$title, method_label),
             subtitle = sprintf("donor%d, n = %s cells", donor_id, format(sum(keep), big.mark = ",")),
             x = sprintf("%s (transformed)", gate$xcol), y = sprintf("%s (transformed)", gate$ycol)) +
        theme_bw(base_size = 10) +
        theme(plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7.5))
}

gating_by_method_root <- file.path(out_dir, "figures", "gating_by_method")
for (cf in cof_names) {
    tr <- transform_raw(get_cofactors(cf))
    for (gate in gate_defs_post_transform) {
        gdir <- file.path(gating_by_method_root, cf, gate$dir)
        dir.create(gdir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
        grid_file <- file.path(gdir, "grid_3col.png")
        if (!file.exists(grid_file)) {
            files <- character(7)
            for (donor_id in 1:7) {
                outfile <- file.path(gdir, sprintf("donor%d.png", donor_id))
                p <- gating_make_plot_transformed(tr, gate, donor_id, cf)
                ggsave(outfile, p, width = 5.5, height = 4.2, dpi = 150)
                files[donor_id] <- outfile
            }
            imgs <- magick::image_read(files)
            montage <- magick::image_montage(imgs, tile = "3x3", geometry = "x450+8+8", bg = "white")
            magick::image_write(montage, grid_file, format = "png")
        }
    }
    rm(tr); gc(FALSE)
}
cat("Post-transform gating figures written under", gating_by_method_root, "\n")
```

```{r gating-figures-by-method-display, results = "asis"}
for (gate in gate_defs_post_transform) {
    cat(sprintf("\n#### %s\n\n", gate$title))
    for (cf in cof_names) {
        grid_file <- file.path(gating_by_method_root, cf, gate$dir, "grid_3col.png")
        cat(sprintf("\n##### %s\n\n", cf))
```
