Stage 1 is a **screen with one seed**: it generates hypotheses, stages 2 and 3
test them. Assigning nodes ourselves costs some time per run (roughly 15-30 s);
the stage can be interrupted and resumed because finished runs are skipped.

```{r stage1}
stage1 <- cached("11_stage1_v2.rds", run_stage(stage1_grid, "stage1_v2"))
cat(sum(!is.na(stage1$error)), "failed runs;", "total compute", round(sum(stage1$runtime_s) / 3600, 2), "h\n")
if (any(!is.na(stage1$error))) print(table(stage1$error))
s <- stage1[!is.na(stage1$ari), ]
```

### How much can a single run resolve? The noise floor

`center_global` and `none` are **mathematically identical** for Manhattan,
Euclidean and Chebyshev (H0), and the engine check confirmed this for the node
assignment. Each such pair therefore measures pure run-to-run noise: same seed,
same initial cells, same data up to a shift. Any ARI difference within a pair is
noise.

```{r noise-floor}
a <- stage1[stage1$scaling == "none", ]
b <- stage1[stage1$scaling == "center_global", ]
twins <- merge(a, b, by = c("cofactor", "batch", "weighting", "distf", "distance"),
               suffixes = c("_none", "_ctr"))
twins$delta_ari <- twins$ari_ctr - twins$ari_none

noise_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(twins, twins$distance), function(d)
    data.frame(distance = d$distance[1], n_pairs = nrow(d),
               pct_identical = 100 * mean(abs(d$delta_ari) < 1e-9),
               median_abs = median(abs(d$delta_ari)),
               p95_abs = unname(quantile(abs(d$delta_ari), 0.95)),
               max_abs = max(abs(d$delta_ari)))))
rownames(noise_tab) <- NULL
noise_band <- unname(quantile(abs(twins$delta_ari[twins$distf != 4]), 0.95))
noise_tab
aggregate(pct_mapping_agree ~ distance, stage1, min)
```

For the three translation-invariant distances, `r round(mean(abs(twins$delta_ari[twins$distf != 4]) < 1e-9) * 100)`%
of the twin pairs are bit-identical, but the others differ by up to
`r round(max(abs(twins$delta_ari[twins$distf != 4])), 3)` ARI. The most likely
reason is that online SOM training is chaotic: a floating-point difference can
flip one nearest-node decision, the trajectories diverge, and the consensus step
may then merge a different pair of populations. H0 is therefore **true as
mathematics but not testable to better than the noise band** of
`r round(noise_band, 3)` (95th percentile of |dARI| over the exact twins).

Consequences for everything below:

* single-run differences smaller than the noise band are not interpreted;
* every factor effect is shown as a **paired difference** (same setting except
  the factor) against that band;
* the marginal means of the earlier version are dropped because they averaged
  over an unbalanced design (`flat_150` has no cyCombine arm);
* `pct_mapping_agree` (table above) says how far FlowSOM's own `mapping` departs
  from our node assignment for each distance.

### Factor effects, paired and against the noise floor

For each factor, every configuration is paired with the same configuration at the
reference level (scaling: `none`; cofactor: `paper`; batch: `none`; weighting:
`none`; distance: `euclidean`), and the difference in ARI is recorded.

```{r paired-effects}
paired_effect <- function(d, f, ref) {
    cfg_f <- if (f == "distance") "distf" else f
    key <- setdiff(cfg_cols, cfg_f)
    lev <- as.character(d[[f]])
    r <- d[lev == ref, c(key, "ari")]; names(r)[names(r) == "ari"] <- "ari_ref"
    o <- d[lev != ref, c(key, f, "ari")]
    m <- merge(o, r, by = key)
    if (nrow(m) == 0L) {
        return(data.frame(factor = character(0), level = character(0),
                          delta = numeric(0), stringsAsFactors = FALSE))
    }
    data.frame(factor = f, level = as.character(m[[f]]), delta = m$ari - m$ari_ref)
}
effects <- rbind(paired_effect(s, "scaling", "none"),
                 paired_effect(s, "cofactor", "paper"),
                 paired_effect(s, "batch", "none"),
                 paired_effect(s, "weighting", "none"),
                 paired_effect(s, "distance", "euclidean"))

effect_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(effects, list(effects$factor, effects$level), drop = TRUE),
    function(d) data.frame(factor = d$factor[1], level = d$level[1], n_pairs = nrow(d),
                           mean_delta = mean(d$delta), median_delta = median(d$delta),
                           pct_better_than_noise = 100 * mean(d$delta > noise_band),
                           pct_worse_than_noise  = 100 * mean(d$delta < -noise_band))))
effect_tab <- effect_tab[order(effect_tab$factor, -effect_tab$mean_delta), ]
rownames(effect_tab) <- NULL
eff <- function(f, l) { v <- effect_tab$mean_delta[effect_tab$factor == f & effect_tab$level == l]
                        if (length(v)) v else NA_real_ }
batch_bullet <- if (have_cycombine) {
    sprintf(paste0(
        "cyCombine moves ARI by %+.3f on average, ",
        "small relative to the band."),
        eff("batch", "cyCombine"))
} else {
    paste("cyCombine was not installed in this session, so the batch factor",
        "has a single level here; its paired effect is reported in the",
        "full-run version of this document.")
}
effect_tab
```

```{r fig-effects, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6}
p <- ggplot(effects, aes(reorder(level, delta, median), delta)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -noise_band, ymax = noise_band,
             fill = "grey80", alpha = 0.5) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.7, fill = "white") + coord_flip() +
    facet_wrap(~factor, scales = "free_y") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Paired change in ARI vs. the reference level",
         title = "Stage 1: effect of each factor level (grey band = noise floor)") +
    theme_minimal()
show_plot(p, "stage1_paired_effects", 9, 6)
```

Reading the figure (written against the first complete run; re-check after
re-running):

* **Scaling is the factor that matters.** `none`, `center_global`, `alpha0.5`
  and `pct_range` are indistinguishable (mean paired change within the grey
  band; `pct_range` `r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("scaling", "pct_range"))`). Full
  equalisation hurts: `zscore` `r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("scaling", "zscore"))`,
  `robust_z` `r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("scaling", "robust_z"))`. H1 is therefore
  only partly right: dividing by the SD hurts, but `pct_range` does not. It uses
  the 1st-99th percentile range, which for noise-only markers is about 4.65 SD,
  so it inflates them much less than a z-score does.
* **Donor-based scaling hurts** (`donor_median`
  `r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("scaling", "donor_median"))`, `donor_z`
  `r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("scaling", "donor_z"))`) and, for `donor_median`, raises
  donor leakage (below). The median of a bimodal marker such as CD3, CD19 or CD56
  is set by the donor's population mix, so centring on it moves T-rich and
  B/NK-rich donors in opposite directions and injects composition instead of
  removing a technical offset. This agrees with the within-population heatmap,
  where most donor offsets are small.
* **Cofactor.** The per-donor CyEt cofactor is the only cofactor strategy that
  is clearly worse than `paper` (`r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("cofactor", "cyet_donor"))`).
  The flat cofactors are within or near the band, consistent with the stage-0
  plateau.
* **Batch.** `r batch_bullet`
* **Weighting.** The oracle weights give `r sprintf("%+.3f", eff("weighting", "sqrt_eta2"))`
  on average, but see the top lists: the gain comes from rescuing poor scalings,
  not from improving good ones.
* **Distance.** Differences between distances are within the band (see ANOVA).

### How the variance splits

Share of the variance in ARI attributable to each factor (sequential sum of
squares; the design is slightly unbalanced because `flat_150` has no cyCombine
arm, so treat it as a rough ranking, not as an exact decomposition):

```{r stage1-anova}
## Only terms whose factors actually vary enter the model: when cyCombine is
## not installed, `batch` has a single level and lm() refuses a constant
## factor (and the cofactor:batch interaction with it).
fac_levels <- vapply(c("cofactor", "batch", "scaling", "weighting", "distance"),
                     function(f) length(unique(stage1[[f]])) > 1L, NA)
an_terms <- c(names(fac_levels)[fac_levels],
    "scaling:distance", "weighting:distance")
if (fac_levels[["cofactor"]] && fac_levels[["batch"]]) {
    an_terms <- c(an_terms, "cofactor:batch")
}
fit <- lm(reformulate(an_terms, response = "ari"), data = stage1)
an <- anova(fit)
an$pct_of_total_SS <- round(100 * an[["Sum Sq"]] / sum(an[["Sum Sq"]]), 1)
an[, c("Df", "Sum Sq", "pct_of_total_SS")]
```

Scaling takes `r an["scaling", "pct_of_total_SS"]`% of the sum of squares and the
residual `r an["Residuals", "pct_of_total_SS"]`%. The residual is not pure noise
(interactions not in the model, such as cofactor x scaling, end up there), but
the twin analysis shows that run-to-run noise alone can reach the size of many
"effects". `scaling:distance` (`r an["scaling:distance", "pct_of_total_SS"]`%)
is tiny compared with `scaling`: scaling acts the same way for all four
distances, which is relevant for H3.

### The full ARI map

```{r heatmap-fun}
heat <- function(w) {
    d <- stage1[stage1$weighting == w, ]
    d$setup <- paste(d$cofactor, d$batch, sep = " | ")
    ggplot(d, aes(scaling, setup, fill = ari)) +
        geom_tile(colour = "white") +
        geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", ari)), size = 2.2) +
        scale_fill_viridis(limits = c(0, 1), na.value = "grey80", name = "ARI") +
        facet_wrap(~distance, nrow = 1) +
        labs(x = "Scaling", y = "Cofactor | batch correction",
             title = paste0("Stage 1: ARI of every pipeline, weighting = ", w, " (seed 1234)")) +
        theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank())
}
```

```{r fig-stage1-heatmap-none, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 4.5}
show_plot(heat("none"), "stage1_ari_heatmap_unweighted", 12, 4.5)
```

```{r fig-stage1-heatmap-oracle, fig.width = 12, fig.height = 4.5}
show_plot(heat("sqrt_eta2"), "stage1_ari_heatmap_oracle", 12, 4.5)
```

### Accuracy vs. ambiguity (within each distance only)

Ambiguity ratios of different distance functions are not strictly comparable,
and the node assignment of non-Euclidean runs was questionable in the first
version. The panels are therefore free-scaled per distance; compare points
**within** a panel only, never the ambiguity level between panels (cosine's low
ambiguity is in particular not evidence for cosine).

```{r fig-stage1-tradeoff, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
p <- ggplot(stage1, aes(pct_ambiguous, ari, colour = weighting)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1.8) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(none = "#264653", sqrt_eta2 = "#dc3545")) +
    facet_wrap(~distance, scales = "free_x", nrow = 1) +
    labs(x = "Ambiguous cells (%)", y = "ARI vs. known population",
         title = "Stage 1: accuracy vs. ambiguity (per distance)") + theme_minimal()
show_plot(p, "stage1_ari_vs_ambiguity", 10, 4)
```

### Donor leakage, read against the floor

The dashed line is `donor_floor`, the `ari_donor` of a perfect clustering.

```{r fig-stage1-donor, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 4.5}
p <- ggplot(stage1, aes(scaling, ari_donor, fill = batch)) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = donor_floor, linetype = "dashed") +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~distance, nrow = 1) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(begin = 0.2, end = 0.8) +
    labs(x = "Scaling", y = "ARI vs. donor", title = "Stage 1: donor leakage (dashed: perfect-clustering floor)") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
show_plot(p, "stage1_donor_leakage", 9, 4.5)
```

The best configurations sit on the floor (leakage = composition only).
`donor_median` and `cyet_donor` lie clearly above it, so they add donor
structure. cyCombine tends to sit at or below the floor, which is expected if it
removes donor structure, but it may also remove composition (see the cautions at
the end).

### Leaders

```{r stage1-top}
show_cols <- c(cfg_cols, "distance", "ari", "ari_node_majority", "ari_donor", "node_purity", "pct_ambiguous")
lf  <- stage1[stage1$weighting == "none" & !is.na(stage1$ari), ]
orc <- stage1[stage1$weighting != "none" & !is.na(stage1$ari), ]
head(lf[order(-lf$ari), show_cols], 15)
head(orc[order(-orc$ari), show_cols], 10)
anchor <- stage1[stage1$cofactor == "paper" & stage1$batch == "none" & stage1$scaling == "none" &
                 stage1$weighting == "none" & stage1$distf == 2, show_cols]
anchor
n_tied <- sum(lf$ari >= max(lf$ari) - noise_band)
```

`r n_tied` label-free configurations lie within the noise band
(`r round(noise_band, 3)`) of the best one, so the "winner" is not distinguished
from the pack. What the leaders have in common is more informative than their
order: which cofactor, whether any batch correction or donor-based scaling is
present, and which scalings appear. The `anchor` row (paper cofactors, nothing
else, Euclidean) is the reference. It is not guaranteed to match the headline
ARI of the earlier vignette, because that one used CATALYST's `cluster()` with
ConsensusClusterPlus, while this one uses `SOM()` plus FlowSOM's
`metaClustering_consensus()`. Compare rows within this document.

## Stage 2: do the finalists survive other seeds?

Finalists: the anchor, the top `r top_k` label-free configurations, the best
label-free configuration **per distance function**, and the top 3 oracle-weighted
configurations. For every finalist that has an exact twin (`none` vs.
`center_global`, non-cosine), the twin is added too: two mathematically identical
runs must agree, so their gap measures noise inside the final comparison. Each is
re-run with the seeds after the first (`r paste(seeds_all[-1], collapse = ", ")`;
seed 1234 is from stage 1).

```{r stage2}
best_by_dist <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(lf, lf$distf), function(d) d[which.max(d$ari), ]))
fin <- unique(rbind(
    stage1[stage1$cofactor == "paper" & stage1$batch == "none" & stage1$scaling == "none" &
           stage1$weighting == "none" & stage1$distf == 2, ],
    head(lf[order(-lf$ari), ], top_k),
    best_by_dist,
    head(orc[order(-orc$ari), ], 3))[, cfg_cols])
twin_of <- c(none = "center_global", center_global = "none")
tw <- fin[fin$scaling %in% names(twin_of) & fin$distf != 4, ]
tw$scaling <- unname(twin_of[tw$scaling])
finalists <- unique(rbind(fin, tw)); rownames(finalists) <- NULL
cat(nrow(finalists), "finalists\n")

stage2_grid <- merge(finalists, data.frame(seed = seeds_all[-1]), by = NULL)
stage2_grid$xdim <- 10; stage2_grid$k <- 12
stage2 <- cached("12_stage2_v2.rds", run_stage(stage2_grid, "stage2_v2"))

reps <- merge(rbind(stage1[, names(stage2)], stage2), finalists, by = cfg_cols)   # finalists only
reps$config <- do.call(paste, c(reps[cfg_cols[1:4]], list(reps$distance), sep = " | "))
stage2_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(reps, reps$config), function(d)
    data.frame(config = d$config[1], weighting = d$weighting[1], n_seeds = nrow(d),
               ari_mean = mean(d$ari), ari_sd = sd(d$ari),
               ari_min = min(d$ari), ari_max = max(d$ari),
               node_majority_mean = mean(d$ari_node_majority),
               ambiguous_mean = mean(d$pct_ambiguous), donor_ari_mean = mean(d$ari_donor))))
stage2_summary <- stage2_summary[order(-stage2_summary$ari_mean), ]
rownames(stage2_summary) <- NULL
## "tied" = not distinguishable from the best config (difference < 2 standard errors)
stage2_summary$tied_with_best <- with(stage2_summary,
    (ari_mean[1] - ari_mean) <= 2 * sqrt((ari_sd / sqrt(n_seeds))^2 + (ari_sd[1] / sqrt(n_seeds[1]))^2))
stage2_summary <- cached("13_stage2_summary_v2.rds", stage2_summary)
stage2_summary
```

**Twin check inside stage 2.** These pairs are mathematically identical, so
any gap in mean ARI, and any gap in seed SD, is noise:

```{r stage2-twins}
reps_tw <- reps[reps$scaling %in% names(twin_of) & reps$distf != 4, ]
tw_mean <- aggregate(ari ~ cofactor + batch + weighting + distance + scaling, reps_tw, mean)
tw_sd   <- aggregate(ari ~ cofactor + batch + weighting + distance + scaling, reps_tw, sd)
names(tw_sd)[names(tw_sd) == "ari"] <- "sd"
tw_all  <- merge(tw_mean, tw_sd)
tw_wide <- reshape(tw_all, idvar = c("cofactor", "batch", "weighting", "distance"),
                   timevar = "scaling", direction = "wide")
tw_wide <- tw_wide[complete.cases(tw_wide), ]
tw_wide$mean_gap <- tw_wide$ari.center_global - tw_wide$ari.none
tw_wide
```

```{r fig-stage2, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5}
lev <- stage2_summary$config[order(stage2_summary$ari_mean)]
stage2_summary$config_f <- factor(stage2_summary$config, lev)
reps$config_f <- factor(reps$config, lev)
p <- ggplot(stage2_summary, aes(config_f, ari_mean, colour = weighting)) +
    geom_point(data = reps, aes(config_f, ari), colour = "grey65", alpha = 0.7, size = 1.2, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
    geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = ari_mean - ari_sd, ymax = ari_mean + ari_sd)) +
    coord_flip() + scale_colour_manual(values = c(none = "#264653", sqrt_eta2 = "#dc3545")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = paste0("ARI (mean +/- SD over ", n_seeds, " seeds; grey: single seeds)"),
         title = "Stage 2: finalists across seeds (red = oracle weights)") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7))
show_plot(p, "stage2_finalists_seeds", 9, 5.5)
```

How to read it:

* **Do not read the order of the table as a ranking.** Differences between
  configurations that are smaller than their seed-to-seed SD should not be
  interpreted. `r sum(stage2_summary$tied_with_best)` of
  `r nrow(stage2_summary)` finalists are statistically tied with the top one.
* **The twin pairs are the calibration.** If two mathematically identical
  configurations differ in mean ARI or in seed SD (table above), that difference
  is what chance alone does at this number of seeds. A small seed SD for one twin
  and a large one for the other is not a property of the scaling: the
  distribution of outcomes is bimodal (the consensus step either merges a pair
  of populations or not), and with few seeds one twin can simply have escaped the
  bad outcome.
* `node_majority_mean` does not depend on metaclustering. If it is nearly
  identical across finalists while `ari_mean` varies, the variation comes from
  the metaclustering step, not from the preprocessing.

## Stage 3: does the ranking transfer to other grid sizes and k?

Finalists are re-run (first `r min(3L, n_seeds)` seeds) at 5x5 and 15x15 grids
with `k` = 12, and at 10x10 with `k` = 8 (the true number of populations) and
`k` = 16. If the ranking holds, the winner is not tuned to a single grid or
number of metaclusters.

```{r stage3}
seeds_s3 <- seeds_all[seq_len(min(3L, n_seeds))]
variants <- data.frame(xdim = c(5, 15, 10, 10), k = c(12, 12, 8, 16))
stage3_grid <- merge(merge(finalists, data.frame(seed = seeds_s3), by = NULL), variants, by = NULL)
stage3 <- cached("14_stage3_v2.rds", run_stage(stage3_grid, "stage3_v2"))

base10 <- merge(rbind(stage1[, names(stage3)], stage2), finalists, by = cfg_cols)   # 10x10, k=12 reference
base10 <- base10[base10$seed %in% seeds_s3, ]
conf <- rbind(base10, stage3)
conf$config  <- do.call(paste, c(conf[cfg_cols[1:4]], list(conf$distance), sep = " | "))
conf$variant <- sprintf("grid %dx%d, k=%d", conf$xdim, conf$xdim, conf$k)
var_levels <- c("grid 5x5, k=12", "grid 10x10, k=8", "grid 10x10, k=12", "grid 10x10, k=16", "grid 15x15, k=12")
conf$variant <- factor(conf$variant, levels = var_levels)

conf_mean <- aggregate(ari ~ config + variant + weighting, conf, mean)
conf_wide <- reshape(conf_mean[, c("config", "variant", "ari")], idvar = "config",
                     timevar = "variant", direction = "wide")
names(conf_wide) <- sub("^ari\\.", "", names(conf_wide))
conf_wide <- conf_wide[, c("config", intersect(var_levels, names(conf_wide)))]
ref_name  <- "grid 10x10, k=12"
conf_wide <- cached("15_stage3_summary_v2.rds", conf_wide[order(-conf_wide[[ref_name]]), ])
conf_wide

variant_best <- do.call(rbind, lapply(setdiff(names(conf_wide), "config"), function(v) {
    x <- conf_wide[[v]]
    data.frame(variant = v, best_config = conf_wide$config[which.max(x)],
               best_ari = max(x), median_ari = median(x), worst_ari = min(x))
}))
variant_best
```

Spearman correlation of the stage-1/2 ranking with the ranking at other
settings. Because the finalists differ by less than the noise band at 10x10, low
correlations are *expected*, so this is only a sanity number. The table above
(spread across finalists per variant) is the more informative result:

```{r stage3-rank}
ref <- conf_wide[[ref_name]]
sapply(setdiff(names(conf_wide), c("config", ref_name)),
       function(v) suppressWarnings(cor(ref, conf_wide[[v]], method = "spearman", use = "complete.obs")))
```

```{r fig-stage3, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5}
p <- ggplot(conf_mean, aes(variant, ari, group = config,
                           colour = ifelse(weighting == "none", "label-free", "oracle"))) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.6) + geom_point() +
    scale_colour_manual(values = c(`label-free` = "#264653", oracle = "#dc3545"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "ARI (mean over seeds)", title = "Stage 3: finalists at other grid sizes and k") +
    theme_minimal() + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 25, hjust = 1))
show_plot(p, "stage3_grid_k_confirmation", 9, 5)
```

**Why does `k` = 8 hurt?** It is the true number of populations but not
necessarily the best `k`. The contingency table of the anchor shows which
populations the consensus step merges or splits at `k` = 8:

```{r k8-diagnostic}
k8_table <- cached("16_k8_contingency_v2.rds", local({
    X <- prepare_X(get_base("paper", "none"), "none", "none")
    set.seed(1234)
    som  <- FlowSOM::SOM(X, xdim = 10, ydim = 10, rlen = 10, mst = 1, distf = 2, silent = TRUE)
    node <- assign_nodes(X, som$codes, 2)
    mc   <- meta_cluster(som$codes, 8, 1234)[node]
    table(metacluster = mc, population = pop)
}), csv = FALSE)
k8_table
```

Read the table row by row: a metacluster spread over several populations is a
merge; a population spread over several rows is a split. The labelled
populations are very unequal in size and the CD4/CD8 T-cell subsets form a
continuum along CCR7/CD45RA, so 8 groups need not coincide with the 8 labels. A
drop in ARI at `k` = 8 is thus a statement about the labels and the
metaclustering step, not necessarily about the preprocessing. Note that stage 3
now uses several seeds, because with one seed a bimodal outcome (merge or no
merge) would look like a systematic difference between configurations.

## Verdict: the questions and hypotheses

The evidence column is computed; the verdict column was written after inspecting
the first complete run and must be re-checked if numbers change after a re-run.

```{r verdict}
best_lf <- lf[which.max(lf$ari), ]
best_or <- orc[which.max(orc$ari), ]
tw_abs  <- tapply(abs(twins$delta_ari), twins$distance, mean)
verdict <- data.frame(
    hypothesis = c("H0", "H1", "H2", "H3", "H4", "H5"),
    evidence = c(
        sprintf("Node assignment translation-invariant for %.2f%% of cells (L1/L2/Linf); end-to-end |dARI| of exact twins: median %.3f, 95th pct %.3f, max %.3f.",
                min(engine_checks$translation_invariant_pct[engine_checks$distance != "cosine"]),
                median(abs(twins$delta_ari[twins$distf != 4])), noise_band,
                max(abs(twins$delta_ari[twins$distf != 4]))),
        sprintf("Paired dARI vs none: zscore %+.3f, robust_z %+.3f, pct_range %+.3f.",
                eff("scaling", "zscore"), eff("scaling", "robust_z"), eff("scaling", "pct_range")),
        sprintf("donor_median: dARI %+.3f, mean ari_donor %.3f vs floor %.3f.",
                eff("scaling", "donor_median"),
                mean(s$ari_donor[s$scaling == "donor_median"]), donor_floor),
        sprintf("Mean |dARI| from centring by distance: %s. scaling:distance = %.1f%% of SS vs scaling = %.1f%%.",
                paste(names(tw_abs), round(tw_abs, 3), collapse = ", "),
                an["scaling:distance", "pct_of_total_SS"], an["scaling", "pct_of_total_SS"]),
        sprintf(paste0("Paired dARI: cyet_donor %+.3f (mean ari_donor %.3f)%s;",
                " best label-free config uses batch = %s."),
                eff("cofactor", "cyet_donor"), mean(s$ari_donor[s$cofactor == "cyet_donor"]),
                if (have_cycombine) sprintf(", cyCombine %+.3f",
                    eff("batch", "cyCombine")) else
                    " (cyCombine not installed in this session)",
                best_lf$batch),
        sprintf("Best oracle ARI %.4f vs best label-free %.4f (difference %+.4f, noise band %.3f); mean paired gain of sqrt_eta2 %+.3f.",
                best_or$ari, best_lf$ari, best_or$ari - best_lf$ari, noise_band, eff("weighting", "sqrt_eta2"))),
    verdict = c(
        "Holds as mathematics (invariance check). End-to-end it can only be tested to the noise band, because SOM training amplifies floating-point differences.",
        "Partly supported: z-score and robust z-score hurt; pct_range does not (its 1-99% range is a milder equalisation).",
        "Rejected: donor-based scalings lower ARI and, for donor_median, raise donor leakage. The offsets are mostly compositional.",
        "Not supported at the available resolution: cosine is not more affected by centring than the exact twins are by noise, and scaling acts alike across distances.",
        "Supported for per-donor CyEt (worse, more leakage). cyCombine does not improve on the best uncorrected pipelines.",
        "No headroom: the oracle weights do not beat the best label-free pipeline beyond noise. They mostly rescue poor scalings."),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
knitr::kable(verdict, format = "pipe")
```

Answers to the five questions of the Overview:

1. **Cofactor.** Any flat cofactor on the plateau (`r plateau[1]`-`r plateau[2]`)
   performs like the hand-tuned per-marker `paper` set. A per-donor,
   normality-driven cofactor (CyEt) is the one strategy that is clearly worse and
   leaks donor structure.
2. **Batch correction.** Donor = batch is not a good model here: donors differ in
   composition, and the best pipelines are all uncorrected. cyCombine is neither
   clearly harmful nor helpful in paired comparisons.
3. **Scaling.** The decision that matters most. No scaling, global centring,
   `alpha0.5` and `pct_range` are equivalent; full equalisation (z-score, robust
   z-score) and donor-based scalings hurt.
4. **Weighting.** Oracle weights add nothing to a good pipeline, so there is no
   room for an unsupervised weighting scheme to gain much on this dataset.
5. **Distance.** Euclidean, Manhattan and Chebyshev are equivalent within noise.
   Cosine is competitive, but its ambiguity values are not comparable with the
   others.

Things to keep in mind when interpreting:

* **Noise first.** Single-run differences below `r round(noise_band, 3)` ARI are not
  interpretable. Use paired effects, stage 2 and stage 3, not the single top
  cell.
* **Selection bias.** The best of hundreds of pipelines, scored on the same labels
  it is selected on, is optimistic.
* **Oracle options** (`flat_<best>`, `sqrt_eta2`) show what is achievable with
  label knowledge. They are not recommendations for unlabeled data.
* **Donor and population are crossed here** (every donor has all 8 populations),
  but with very different cell counts. Corrections that equalise donors
  (cyCombine, `donor_median`, `donor_z`) can remove real composition signal as
  well as technical offsets. Compare `ari_donor` with `donor_floor`, and use the
  within-population donor-SD heatmap as the evidence to weigh against ARI.
* **Non-Euclidean distances** use FlowSOM's default learning schedule and
  Euclidean metaclustering, and their node assignment is our own (see the engine
  checks), so they are exploratory.
* **ARI depends on `k` and on the labels.** The 8 labels are not equally
  separable, so ARI differences at a fixed `k` partly reflect the metaclustering
  step.
* Extensions that fit the same engine: add a pooled CyEt vector to `cof_registry`
  (a named numeric vector of 24 cofactors), add unsupervised marker weights (e.g.
  bimodality-based) to `apply_weights()`, add other scalings to
  `apply_scaling()`, or test whether the CCR7 donor offsets follow the fluorophore
  swap (donors 1-4 vs 5-7).

## CySA on the labelled data: nodes against the known gating

Everything above judged whole pipelines with global numbers: ARI against the
known gating, mean node purity, the share of ambiguous cells. That is the
batch view; it says how good a pipeline is, not *where* it goes wrong. The
interactive view is per node: which nodes mix two labels, how close their
cells sit to a rival node, and what to do about them. This section runs
CySA's own functions on the anchor SOM to show the bridge. No new method is
introduced; the point is that the object CySA expects -- an SCE with
`SOM_codes`, `SOM_stats` and `cluster_id` -- is exactly what this document
already builds, and the known gating plugs in as one extra column.

```{r cysa-sce}
#' Anchor SOM once, packaged the way the CyDa pipeline hands it to CySA.
cysa_anchor <- cached("cysa_anchor_som.rds", local({
    Xbase <- get_base("paper", "none")
    X <- prepare_X(Xbase, "none", "none")
    set.seed(1234)
    som  <- FlowSOM::SOM(X, xdim = 10, ydim = 10, rlen = 10, mst = 1,
        distf = 2, silent = TRUE)
    node <- assign_nodes(X, som$codes, 2)
    list(som = som, node = node, X = X)
}), csv = FALSE)
som <- cysa_anchor$som; node <- cysa_anchor$node; X <- cysa_anchor$X

rownames(som$codes) <- as.character(seq_len(nrow(som$codes)))
sce <- SingleCellExperiment::SingleCellExperiment(
    assays = list(exprs = t(X)),
    colData = S4Vectors::DataFrame(
        sample_id = paste0("donor", donor),
        cluster_id = factor(node, levels = seq_len(nrow(som$codes))),
        cell_type = pop
    )
)
S4Vectors::metadata(sce)$SOM_codes <- som$codes
S4Vectors::metadata(sce)$map <- list(colsUsed = type_m)
SingleCellExperiment::int_metadata(sce)$channels <-
    S4Vectors::DataFrame(channel_name = type_m, marker_name = type_m)
```

`cell_type` is the only addition over the CyDa layout: the known gating, read
back into the object, so every SOM node can be scored against it.
`prepClusterSelectorData(..., cellTypeCol = "cell_type")` derives the per-node
label summary (`node_labels`: majority label and purity) on the *full* object
and draws the stratified subsample the app's plots use. The tables show the
two ends of the purity ranking:

```{r cysa-prep}
prepped <- CySA::prepClusterSelectorData(sce, total_cells_to_sample = 50000,
    cellTypeCol = "cell_type")
nl <- S4Vectors::metadata(prepped$sce)$node_labels
n_pure  <- sum(nl$purity >= 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)
n_mixed <- sum(nl$purity < 0.90, na.rm = TRUE)
head(nl[order(-nl$purity), ])
mixed <- nl[!is.na(nl$purity) & nl$purity < 0.90, ]
mixed[order(mixed$purity), ]
```

`r n_pure` of the `r nrow(nl)` nodes are essentially pure (purity >= 0.95) and
`r n_mixed` fall below 0.90; purity is NA for the nodes that hold no
labeled cells in the full object. Pure nodes are the expectation: a 100-node
SOM on well-separated
cytometry populations places most nodes inside one population. The mixed rows
are the interesting ones, and this document's earlier diagnostics predict
where they come from: the naive -> memory -> TEMRA axis is a continuum, so its
boundary nodes mix adjacent subsets no matter how the grid is laid out; the
mis-routing diagnostics showed the largest cell-level pull comes from dim,
variable CD56 on T cells (with CD8 next); and the CCR7/HELIOS fluorophore swap
gives donors 5-7 a different CCR7 pedestal, so nodes that separate naive from
memory partly split by donor instead. Five of the six mixed nodes are
naive/TEMRA boundary nodes, and in all five the majority label flips between
donor groups: the pedestal shift moves the same node to one side of the
continuum in donors 1-4 and to the other in donors 5-7. A donor-split node can
also be label-pure but cohort-split; those do not show in this table (their
label purity is 1) but appear in the marker views below as same-label nodes
sitting at different CCR7 positions.

```{r cysa-views, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6.2}
p1 <- CySA::plotSOMScatter(prepped$sce, chs = c("CCR7", "CD45RA"),
    color_by = "purity")
show_plot(p1, "cysa_som_ccr7_cd45ra_purity", 7, 6.5)

p2 <- CySA::plotNodeProps(prepped$sce,
    ambiguity = CySA::nodeAmbiguity(prepped$sce_subsampled))
show_plot(p2, "cysa_node_properties", 8, 6)
```

The first view is what the app's SOM 2D plots show: every node at its
CCR7 x CD45RA position, coloured by purity, sized by cell count. Nodes with
purity ~ 1 are single known populations; the low-purity ones sit where the
continuum runs and where the donor pedestal shifts CCR7. The second view is
the node-properties plane (purity against cell count, with the ambiguity
columns `medianRatio`/`pctAmbiguous` computed by `nodeAmbiguity()` and joined
by node id). This is the operational answer to the usefulness question: the
analyst does not scroll through 100 nodes one by one -- they look at the
low-purity / high-ambiguity corner, lasso those nodes (in the app this plot
is wired to the node selection, so a lasso there selects nodes everywhere),
and investigate them in the marker views. The decision that follows --
drop a marker, refine the SOM below a node, or accept the mixed node as the
honest boundary of the continuum -- is exactly the hierarchical refinement
this document's diagnostics motivated.

## Output manifest and session information

```{r manifest}
files <- list.files(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
files <- files[!grepl("^runs/", files)]
data.frame(file = files,
           size_MB = round(file.size(file.path(out_dir, files)) / 1e6, 2))
cat(length(list.files(file.path(out_dir, "runs"), recursive = TRUE)),
    "individual run files in", file.path(out_dir, "runs"), "\n")

cached("00_config_v2.rds", list(params = params, n_cores = n_cores, N = N, type_markers = type_m,
    cofactor_sets = cof_names, cycombine_sets = if (have_cycombine) cc_sets else NULL,
    scalings = scalings, best_flat_cofactor = best_cf, n_seeds = n_seeds,
    donor_floor = donor_floor, noise_band = noise_band, date = Sys.time()),
    csv = FALSE) -> cfg_saved

si_file <- file.path(out_dir, "99_session_info.txt")
if (!file.exists(si_file)) writeLines(capture.output(sessionInfo()), si_file)
sessionInfo()
```
